Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister), for the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 138, to amend and consolidate the Acts relating to British Nationality, Naturalization and Aliens. He said:	The provisions of the
main Act and of the amendments now' being consolidated are well known to hon. members of the House. The purpose of the present Bill is:
(1)	To consolidate the present Canadian Naturalization Acts of 1914, and 5 Geo. V, chapter 7.
(2)	To incorporate therewith the provisions of the Imperial Act of 1914 as amended by the Imperial Act of 1918.
The main provisions in the new Bill are as follows: Provision is made for the revocation of certificates of naturalization heretofore granted in Canada.
(a)	Where such certificates have been obtained1 by fraud, misrepresentation or concealment of material facts.
(b)	where the holder of the certificate has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty;
(c)	v'here the holder of the certificate has during the war unlawfully traded with the enemy, etc.;

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKBNZIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext: I quite understand that this motion is not debatable, but I should like to state to the Prime Minister that this Bill strikes me as being of very far-reaching effect and of the greatest possible importance, and I fear it is being introduced at too late a stage in the session. If it could possibly stand over until another session I think it would be more satisfactory to Parliament and to the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION ACT.
speechtext:
The Naturalization Act of 1914 was based upon a resolution reached at the Imperial Conference of 1911. That resolution had for its purpose the fixing of uniform standards of naturalization throughout the various Dominions of the Empire, and the granting of certificates of naturalization Which would be effective, not only in the country in which they were granted, as was the case previously, but throughout the whole Empire.
The Act passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom on that occasion was adopted in Canada after a great deal of 
correspondence and negotiation, and I understand it has also been adopted in Newfoundland. It was to be brought before the parliaments of Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa immediately before the war, but I understand that owing to the war the measure has not been proceeded with in those countries. The purpose of this Bill is to render our Act uniform with that of the United Kingdom, and its provisions are framed with that object. I do not think we have departed in any important respect whatever from the principles embodied in the Imperial Act of last year. My hon. friend suggests delay, but I do not think that a fair examination of the Bill will support any reason which could be advanced therefor. It is extremely important that the Act should he made uniform with that of the United Kingdom, and it is also of the utmost importance that the proposals to which I have very briefly alluded, and which will be found in the provisions of the Bill, should be carried into effect in this country at the earliest opportunity. speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment of Mr. McMaster thereto (resumed from Tuesday, June 17).

Mr. Speaker, in rising in this House for the first time to make a few remarks, I feel 1 should almost .apologize to you. Sir, and the hon. members of the House for the fact that in so doing I am breaking a precedent of long standing. In the short time I have been here I have come to regard precedent with considerable respect and reverence, and I think you will appreciate my position under the present circumstances. The precedent to which I have reference is one that was created by the hon, gentleman (Mr. Champagne), who preceded me in the representation of Battleford constituency. I believe that this is the first time that the people of that constituency have had an opportunity of having their views expressed in this House.
Before proceeding to a consideration of the subjects under discussion, I feel it my duty to make a few observations on the past record of the Government. I believe there are very few western members who have had the opportunity that I have had to observe just what has been going on at Ottawa, particularly during recess. I think it is only fair to state, in view of the prevailing criticism in the country, that it is my firm belief that the hon. gentlemen who occupy the Cabinet benches at the present time have made an honest effort to prosecute the war to a successful issue, facing difficulties which were very considerable indeed, and in the solution of which they had absolutely nothing in the way of precedent to assist them. I think I should go a
.'>588

little further and express to the hon. the Prime Minister my heartfelt thanks for the stand he has taken during the latter years of his parliamentary career.
I am sure that the country owes him a great debt of gratitude because in all the trying times that he has been through, more particularly in the last two or three years, he has never wavered in one particular in his loyalty and devotion to the country, and as a loyal Canadian I appreciate that very much. With all that has been done with reference to the carrying on of the war, and bringing it to a successful conclusion, I am in hearty accord.
Before dealing with the Budget, which is agitating my mind particularly at this moment, and I think also the mind of every member of this House, I would like to refer to another matter which has been, and is at present, a subject of very great concern to the farmers of the West. I am a farmer myself, it is the only occupation I have and my only source of livelihood, and I wish to state here that the interests of the farmers are my interests. In years gone by we have had a great amount of difficulty in marketing our grain. By that I mean, we have had great difficulty in obtaining the prices for our grain that were coming to us. We have always found- those of us rwho were fighting financial adversity, and a great many of us are doing that to-day-that about the time we were forced to sell our grain we were absolutely at the mercy of a bunch of unscrupulous speculators who controlled the grain market- I do not think I am over-stating the case in using such strong language. These people knew perfectly well that at a certain season of the year we had to sell our grain in order to meet our liabilities, and it seemed to us, and it seems to me now, that by some means the price of grain was always forced down, to catch those who were compelled to sell. The only man who had the opportunity of getting a fair return for the grain that he raised was the man who was in good financial circumstances and could hold his crop over until another year. The first relief that we obtained came when the price of grain was set by the Government. Before dilating further upon the selling price of grain, I wish to make myself clear on that point.
I am not advocating the fixing of the price of wheat as a principle-I do not believe that I could conscientiously do so. We have to choose between either protection or a measure, at any rate, of free trade. I have made n>y choice in that 
regard and it has been along the lines of no very great degree of protection. What is in the minds of us farmers of the West at the present time in regard to the wheat crop is the peculiar position we are placed in- Belief, as I 'have already said, came to us when the price was set and we found that we got a fair return for oui crop. That enabled the farmers to go ahead in the fall and prepare their land for the next year without being compelled to rush to the market with their grain to * get it marketed. The setting of the price stabilized the market and stabilized the farming industry.
Now what I would like to impress upon the Government at the present time is the danger of a return to the old conditions which are nothing short of disastrous to the farming industry in Western Canada. I cannot suggest at the present time exactly what course should be pursued, but I would draw the attention of the Government to the fact that something should be done, in view of the peculiar circumstances in which we are placed, to stabilize this industry, which is, if not. the most important, one of the most important, industries of the country. In this connection I would like to read a resolution that was passed at a joint meeting of five local Grain Growers' Associations held at the town of Luseland, Saskatchewan, a month ago, bearing on this question:
Whereas: the economic condition of Canada is very unsettled and a large portion of the 1918 wheat crop is still in the Dominion:
Whereas, the farmers produced, that crop at unusual expense and at the request of the Government and incurred a large expense in preparing the land for the coming wheat crop ;
And whereas, when the conditions were normal, grain buyers were able to so manipulate the market, that they paid a minimum price to the producer and disposed of their holdings at an excessive price to the consumer;
And whereas, the present impoverished condition of the western farmer and the stern necessities of the consumer, will afford those engaged in manipulating- prices an opportunity to press both the producer and consumer;
And whereas, we are convinced that the Government can stabilize the price without serious financial loss and greatly to the advantage of both consumer and producer;
Therefore, resolved that we respectfully request the Government to fix a minimum price for the 1919 wheat crop to correspond with the price fixed by the United States Government.
I thought I should place this resolution on record which was passed at a very large meeting of the grain growers' associations in my constituency, and which is only one of a great many resolutions on the same subject which I have received.
Now, coming to the subject of the Budget.
I find myself in a very difficult posi-

tion. I represent a rather large constituency in the province of Saskatchewan. It is true that I come from the Conservative party, but that does not seem to make any difference in Saskatchewan when the matter is one affecting the tariff. It may be argued that as an old Conservative I could very easily accept the measure of reduction set forth in the Budget by the Finance Minister. But there is another phase to the question from my standpoint which is entirely personal and which is giving me great concern. For years I have travelled up and down the constituency of Battleford before I ever had any thought of being interested in politics, or before anybody else had any idea that I would be in the position in which I am to-day. I expressed certain views to my fellow citizens of that constituency, and I expressed them in no uncertain way, and I am afraid that my action at this time may be construed by these good people to mean that on the very first occasion when the sentiments I had enunciated at home were put to the test down here, that I have utterly failed. If I could make up my mind that there is any alternate course, if there was any way to enter a more vigorous protest without placing myself in a rather inconsistent position, I would have no hesitation in saying that I would have voted against the Budget proposals.
Looking over the amendment of the hon. member for Brome, I find many things in it which appeal to me very strongly. That is true in regard to the first three paragraphs of the amendment, and it is after great effort that I shall have to vote against that amendment. If I believed, or if I could see anything in the past record of hon. gentlemen opposite at this moment-if there was anything in their past record since I came into this House that would appeal to me and make me believe that the amendment was actuated by any spirit of sincerity, I would have no hesitation whatever in supporting it; but I do not believe there is one ounce of sincerity in the amendment; I do not believe that if we had a change of government to-morrow the tariff would be lowered one per cent more on any item than it has been under the Budget proposals presented by the Minister of Finance. Whatever the course that I am pursuing at the present time may lead to from a personal standpoint, I want hon. members in this House and those who are interested in my action in my own constituency, to understand that my course is actuated by
thoroughly conscientious motives and that I am doing what I believe to be in the best interests of my own constituency and of the country at large. I do not wish to attribute any motives, or any desire to be considered as displaying heroism, or anything of that kind, to any hon. gentlemen from 'Western Canada who do not see eye to eye with me.
I would just like to add that there is only one thing that gives me a sort of flickering light of hope in ithe stand I have taken. The hon. member for Red De-eT (Mr. Clark) during the course of his speech on the Budget made the following statement:
I cannot quite agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar)-and this is the only disagreement I shall have with him-in describing the Budget as a protectionist Budget. I think a fairer thing would be lo define it-and I think history will so define it-as a Budget tending towards free trade. I am particularly grateful for the Budget. There was a time when I was charged with being the only free trade member of this House, but to-day, Sir, I am in the proud position of seeing a Government bring down into this House a Budget which proposes to lo-sver tariffs.
I would not for one moment have the audacity to question my hon. friend's judgment on tariff matters; I say that in all sincerity. If he can see in -this Budget evidences of a definite reduction in the tariff-and we are promised by the Minister of Finance a commission to thoroughly investigate the tariff -and make a report at the next session-I do not see that I can do anything under Ithe circumstances but support the Budget.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (Waterloo North): It is not my purpose to speak at any great Length on the subjects that have been under debate. Like the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Wright),
I also am placed in a somewhat perplexing situation, although for another reason. It is not, Sir, because I have any doubts with regard to the Budget itself. I am opposed to the Budget for the -things it does, and I am still more opposed to it for the things that it does not do.
So far as the amendment is concerned, I am entirely in sympathy with a good deal of it, but I may say at the outset that its recommendations with regard to our fiscal policy, while very general in their nature, will, I believe, be interpreted-at least, in the constituency which I have the honour -to represent-as going a little further than my people care to go. In its condemnation of ithe extravagance of the Government, of its failure to -deal with the question of free food for the people, in its
359U

criticisms of the Government for doing nothing to bring down the cost of living,
I am in absolute accord with it.
I was in the House the other evening when the hon. President of the Privy Council made his speech, and if there was one thing that came with something of a shock to me, it was his apparent lack of ability to realize that this Government has a responsibility with regard to the cost of living. He stated that it was just as impossible for the Government to bring back to life the 60,000 Canadian 'soldiers who were slain in the war as to bring down the cost of living. That surely is an appalling confession for a minister of the Crown to make -a confession of weakness and unfitness without parallel. If that is the feeling of the Government, why was a committee appointed to investigate the causes for the increased cost of living-a committee that was supposed to make recommendations to the Government upon which action might be taken to reduce that cost of living? And yet, Sir, while the Government apparently has merely, in vulgar parlance, passed the buck to the committee, in order to evade responsibility, that committee elicited some important facts when it found that the 'Dominion Textile Company-

impossible. Our national debt is $2,000,000,000. To pay the interest on that debt and to carry on the affairs of this country will require an annual expenditure of $300, 000,000. At least some of this money must be raised by a, tariff. Unfortunately, the tariff usually strikes those who are least able to bear the burden, as may be said of other taxation methods of this Government -with which I shall not deal at this time. In the presence of the Finance Minister, I say that the tariff as now constituted seems to me to be a hodge-podge, hit-and-miss sort of contrivance, built up neither for. revenue, nor, as is evident if you examine it carefully, for the advancement of industry. It is unnecessarily high in many cases, and it actually operates to hamper industry in others.
In this connection, I wish to refer for a moment to the constituency which I represent, North Waterloo. We have three large manufacturing centres. The largest of these is the city of Kitchener; we have the town of Waterloo and the village or town of Elmira. In these centres there are from 150 to 175 manufacturing establishments, employing thousands of working people whose prosperity is absolutely dependent upon their employment in these factories. It is not too much to say that these industries were built up under the tariff. I desire to make it quite clear that I have no intention consciously at any time to do anything that would endanger the prosperity of the industries in the riding which I represent, or imperil the employment of the people w 11c>
work in those establishments.
I would not care to take any drastic action in the way of tariff revision the effect of which I cannot estimate without careful investigation. I believe, in many cases, the tariff is too high; that.it fosters combines, the high cost of living and the oppression of the consumer. I believe in a very moderate tariff for development and revenue, and none at all for monopoly. An extremely high tariff creates monopolies, it makes for unduly large profits in which the workingmen do not share. It increases the cost of living, and because of the latter fact, it strikes right hack at the workingman himself, who too often forgets that he also is a consumer. Then again, if you have too high a tariff, you receive no revenue whatever from it because all importation is stopped. I have discussed the mattei with a good many manufacturers in my constituency, and while they are nearly all tariff men, they say, in every instance, that a duty of thirty-five to forty-two and-a-hali 
per cent is altogether higher than is necessary. I am very sorry that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) did not see his way clear to wipe out entirely the seven and-a-half per cent war tax. I do not favour feeding high protective pap for long periods to industries that never will be adapted to this country. That is like trying to grow lemons in Saskatchewan or Alberta; it cannot be done profitably, but you can grow mighty fine wheat in those provinces. It may he that one-day, when the federation of the world is accomplished and all boundary lines are wiped out, that the nations and the peoples of the world will no longer need to trouble themselves about tariffs. Then trade and commerce will find their natural channels, and industry and manufacturing will locate themselves in proximity to raw materials, with regard to suitable markets and to labour conditions. That would make for efficiency and should ultimately benefit both consumer and producer, but that day is not yet. In the meantime, I believe the tariff can be improved, and improved downward in many respects, but I want to see the question dealt with intelligently after careful investigation. Let a careful survey of the whole situation be made, and then let action be taken with full knowledge of the facts. A commission such as the Minister of Finance has proposed should comprise members of all classes in this country and not merely the moneyed interests.	On that board,
in	addition to the	minister himself, there should be at least one representative of agriculture, one of labour, one of industry, and the ordinary consumer should not toe forgotten. Then, whenever and wherever combines or monopolies or inordinate profits are discovered, the tariff ought to toe adjusted without fear or favour according to the facts.
In the riding which I represent we have a large city population, with many people engaged in our factories, and a smaller farming population. I should like to make the point that, just as the prosperity of the farmers in my constituency is closely bound up with that of the industrial population in the towns in that constituency, so in the final analysis, if I understand the situation properly, is the interest of the western farmer and that of the eastern manufacturer dependent the one upon the other. In a country of diversified interests, it is absolutely necessary that there should be some give and take, and some compromise.
I said some time ago that the tariff is framed in this country so as to hamper in-

dustry. That must be so when customs duties are charged on raw materials entering into manufactured products. In the constituency of North Waterloo, which specializes in many lines, we have something like twenty-five furniture manufacturing establishments. As many hon- members may not know, fine lumber and the veneers used in the making of furniture are largely imported from the United States. That lumber includes oak, walnut, mahogany, gumwood and others. For example, just to show the disability under which the Canadian furniture manufacturer would work against a United States manufacturer if there were no tariff, the United States manufacturer pays $135 for 1,000 feet of oak. The Canadian manufacturer pays the same invoice price, but to that he must add the exchange which would be against him just now on the basis of 3 per cent, an amount of $4.05. He must pay freight amounting to $15, and then on top of that the Minister of Finance makes him pay $10.12 in the form of a war tax.. That makes a total of $29.17 extra, or something like 21 per cent on the invoice price of his goods- I do not see what passible justification there can be, when no special Canadian industry would be prejudiced by the removal of that tax, why it should still be maintained.
According to the new Budget proposals, agricultural implements coming into the country will now pay a duty of from 15 to 17^ per cent, not a very high duty; indeed, not higher than the reciprocity pact of 1911 called for. The actual protection is really less than that, because a duty is also charged on certain parts which go into the manufacture of agricultural implements. That at least is the case in the industries in the riding which I represent.
In my city, that of Kitchener, there is a very humble article of manufacture, that of buttons, upon which article, however, a great responsibility Very often depends1.
All the buttons manufactured
12 noon, in Canada are, I think, produced in the city of Kitchener or the town of Waterloo. The raw material from which buttons are manufactured is the nuts of southern countries; it is not produced in Canada, and yet upon that raw material there is the 7j per cent duty to pay. The point I want to make is this, that the addition of that unnecessary duty, as I call it, adds to the cost of the necessaries of life. The consumer has to pay more because of the tariff without any corresponding benefit to the manufacturer. Button
making machinery is very expensive, and is absolutely necessary for the economical production of buttons. It is not made in Canada. Yet upon button making machinery, there is a heavy duty which is all the more trying in face of the keen competition in buttons that is now provided by the Japanese manufacturer who has the advantage of cheap labour.
I see no reason whatever why the tariff on raw materials and food should not be removed, because if that were done, the consumer would be assisted and industry could not be injured.
I have spoken, Mr. Speaker, at greater length than I intended. My friends, I regret, may not altogether appreciate the reasons why I cannot support the amendment. But it goes further than I would care to go without very careful investigation. I believe that in taking this stand I am following the wishes of my consitu-ents, and that is my first care. I shall vote, therefore, against the amendment for two main reasons; First, in view of the large amount of revenue that we must raise in this country in the coming years, I think it is absolutely essential for us to have a moderate tariff. Secondly, I should not like to lend myself to the taking of any action that might interfere with the prosperity of any legitimate industry in my constituency or any where else in Canada without proper investigation. After that investigation has been made, and wherever it is found that the tariff may be reduced with fairness to all concerned, I shall be glad to support any movement in. that direction.
I trust that my action in this regard will not for one moment be understood as expressing support of the Government; it is not intended in that way at all. I shall also vote against the Budget, which I trust I shall have an opportunity of doing, for the reasons I have given, and for the chief reason that I have no confidence in the Government which has brought it down.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to state my position on the Budget proposals and the amendment. My position is rather a peculiar one, in that I am opposed both to the Budget and to the amendment. Unfortunately, the rules of the House do not permit the western democrats to introduce as our fiscal policy the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. I wish, however, to give credit to the Minister of Finance for the very advanced step which he has taken in introducing direct taxation in the form of income tax. That is a plank from the

.3504

platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, and as a member of that body I give him credit for it. I think, however, that he should have made the grades a little more drastic. I notice that the income tax schedules of the United States, if I have read them aright, are very much higher than ours. In Canada on an income of $3,000, the taxation as laid down in the Budget would be $20, whereas on the same income in the United States the tax would be $60. I shall not read all the schedules, but will give four more, to show the House how our taxation compares with theirs. In Canada on an income of $6,000 the tax is $140, in the United States $250; on an income of $20,000 in Canada the tax is $1,382, in the United States $2,630; on an $75,000 income in Canada the tax is $11,007, in the United States $21,350; on a $500,000 income in Canada the tax is $195,407, in the United States $323,000. Therefore, on incomes totalling up this sum the taxation in Canada amounts to $^5,822, whereas in the United States it amounts to $493,770, making a difference in favour of the United States system of $207,948.

I am very glad that he is, and perhaps it is better that he should hear my remarks than read them to-morrow in Hansard. I want to tell him that his action is preventing many a poor child in the three Prairie Provinces from eating apples. The child's acquaintance with this delicious fruit is not a very tangible one, ' for it sees nothing but painted apples. It asks its mother for some apples and the mother says: "We cannot buy you apples, my dear, because they are now dearer by 30 cents on the box." I am of the opinion that when the hon. member for Fraser Valley goes home and closes his door, and in the quiet seclusion of his room contemplates his past actions, he will confess that he is really the cause of poor children of the Prairie Provinces being deprived of apples because of the 30 cents extra that he must have. The hon. member must have his last pound of flesh, no matter who goes without apples.
The hon. member for South Waterloo is, I understand, a very extensive manufacturer of boots and shoes, and I believe is very wealthy. Unlike myself, he had a great deal of fault to find with the Minister of Finance for introducing the income tax system. Now it is quite evident that my surmise as to the hon, gentleman's financial position must be correct, because that system only taxes those who have the wherewithal to pay. Therefore, the hon. gentleman must be wealthy, because he says that it is going to tax him more heavily than the customs taxation must be doing. That is natural, of course, because in the application of the customs tariff to my good friend from South Waterloo before the federal treasury receives one dollar from my good friend from South Waterloo, he, as a manufacturer, has put $3 in his pocket.

eminent. They are, I think, put in a most uncomfortable state of mind. They enter into a contract with the producers of sugar beets to raise a specified quantity of beets and they say: If sugar is worth $8 a hundred we will give you $9 a ton for your beets; if sugar advanced another dollar on the markets in Montreal we shall increase that grant to you by one dollar extra for every ton of beets you deliver to the factories. What is the result of this arrangement? It has produced satisfaction and engendered a feeling of confidence on the part of the subsugar beet producers, and this year they are in the proud position of having hundreds of acres more subscribed for than the factory registered. .If the pork producers had the same confidence in the packers, the Government would not to-day be charged with responsibility for the great shortage there is in meat products. I stand to-day exactly where I stood two years ago on the question of the nationalization of our cold storage systems. I believe that all these systems should be nationalized, and should be under Government control. This is my attitude in regard to this question and for that reason I am opposed to the appointment of any commission to regulate the cost of living in this country. It would mean a further expenditure of thousands of dollars to do nothing but hear complaints. We have too many commissions in Canada and at too great an expense to i the country, and I repeat that our cold storage systems shofild be under Government control. The people could be given such food stuffs as might be placed in these cold storages, plus a fair revenue for keeping them until such time as they were necessary for consumption. I would go further and advocate, in connection with such concerns as pork
packers, creameries and manufacturers of such other lines of goods as are staple necessities the appointment of Government prosecutors instead of more judges and commissions. We should have Government prosecutors and in every case in which unfair profits were extracted from the consumers the offenders should be brought before the superior courts in the various provinces and prosecuted and the unfair profits taken from them. Not very long ago we heard a great deal about the conscription of man power in the country. Well, has there been anything before this House more glaring than the statement from previous speakers that the Textile Company of Montreal made 31 per cent, and the announcement in yesterday's paper that the Paton Manufacturing Company had made 72 per cent? What was said before the committee in reply to a question that was asked one man? I will read from the paper.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member cannot evade the rule by reading from a newspaper. Evidence taken before a Committee of the House cannot be read.

I am willing to wait for the statement from the committee, so far as that is concerned. But when these things are recurring not in one particular line of business but in others, and enormous profits are being rolled up by corporations, may I not call the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the fact that we conscripted our man power and sent them overseas and are failing to conscript the enormous wealth that is being amassed by these concerns. There was a solemn promise by different hon. gentlemen who took a stand in favour of the Military Service Act that they would see that wealth would be conscripted. That was their pledge to the people, and what has been done in that regard? Can you imagine, Sir, the unrest, dissatisfaction, and discouragement that will be felt by the men on their return from overseas when, with the few paltry dollars that they will have in their pockets they go into stores and find that a suit of clothes costs three times as much as when they went overseas to defend the very institutions that have waxed rich while they suffered in Europe? In view of the unrest that prevails I say it is the duty of Parliament to see that a square deal is given these men to whom we pledged our hearty support in this House of Commons when they went overseas. The Minister of Finance made the statement that he was going to save seventeen million odd dollars by reductions in the tariff on agri-
[DOT] >604

cultural implements [DOT] and other things. Well, I do not believe that he was serious when he made that statement. The hon. minister knows that the duty levied against agricultural implements during the past few years has been so prohibitive as to preclude the introduction of a sufficient number of them to assist to any great extent in increased production and thereby tend to the reduction of the high cost of living. He knows, as well as he is aware of the fact that he is Minister of Finance, that we have had very few implements coming into this country to assist in greater-production on account of the high tariff, and consequently there was less production than there would be if the tariff were sufficiently reasonable to allow these implements to come in.
Now what has happened? We have a prohibitive tariff against the machinery necessary to produce more foodstuffs in this country and what has it meant? It has meant, Sir, that every article that is required on the farm, such as harrows, have doubled in price. Land rollers have doubled in price; manure spreaders have doubled in price; grain drills have doubled in price; all kinds of cultivators have doubled in price; disc harrows have doubled in price. The only machinery that has not doubled in price are grain binders and mowing machines upon which the tariff is lower. But there has been an advance on binders of $100 and possibly $40 on mowing machines. The only machine coming in free of duty when the tariff was raised to the high protective point was cream separators referred to by the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) the other day. But when the hon. gentleman made that reference, with all his eloquence he forgot the most important part of -the argument, that cream separators are made to-day by Canadian manufacturers who are competing with the American manufacturers in all parts of the world. Let me add this further: When cream separators were on the free list and when the tariff went up on all other articles to which I have referred and was doubled in price, the cream separator remained at practically the same price from 1914 until 1919.
I want to call the attention of the Government and the Minister of Finance to the fact that if we are to reduce the high cost of living and to produce more foodstuffs to the advantage of both the farmer and the consumer, these matters must be given more consideration than they have received in the past.
[Mr. McColg.l
Now let me take up the article of tractors. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) stated the other night that the Government did a wrong thing when it brought tractors into this country free of duty. In my opinion the action of the Government in importing tractors and selling them at wholesale rates was justified, and I believe it had the effect of increasing production in this country at that time. The hon. member for Brantford has stated that such action was inadvisable, but as the mover of the first resolution introduced into Parliament for the free admission of tractors, I want to say that I stated then and I repeat now that the object of bringing in those tractors free of duty was to assist in increased production. At	that	time I	wasquite satisfied,	as	Hansard	will
show, to amend my resolution so as to include 8-16 and 12-20 horse-power tractors which were not made in Canada but were absolutely the kind, weight, and size ol tractors the most essential to the producers of food stuffs, especially in Ontario. Now, Sir, what has happened ? We had the hon. member for Brantford stating the other night 'that he was not satisfied with that size of tractor, that they were not made in this country, and that they were tractors of larger size that were-the 15-30 horsepower tractor. The 15-30 horse-powei tractor is the one that was referred to by the hon. gentleman. But that is a tractor of too large a size to be used for production in the province of Ontario, but it would do for other work than farm work. The hon. gentleman made the statement on the occasion referred to that there was an undervaluation of these tractors, and that they were being admitted to this country at a valuation of $1,400 and were being sold to the consumers of Canada at a greatly enhanced price. That is apparently true. We find that in the city of Ottawa the Advance Rumely Company have employed a gentleman of the name of Mr. John Bain to act as their agent. That gentleman went to the Minister of Customs, whom I am sorry is not in his seat, and obtained from the Commissioner of Customs permission to bring in 14-28 horse-power tractors to the number of 400. I am of the opinion-the Minister of Custopis can correct me if 1 am wrong-'that no person expects a 14-28 horse-power tractor to be brought in free of duty, because it is the size that is produced by our Canadian manufacturers. However, Mr. Bain obtained consent to bring in 400 of these tractors, and when he found out how easy it was to do that he got the same permision extended to 16-32

horse-power tractors, which is a much larger and much more expensive machine selling in the neighbourhood of from $2,400 to $2,500. He brought those tractors in at a valuation of $1,400 and sold them to the farmers of the West at from $2,200 to $2,500, making a spread of $1,000. That was what the producers of foodstuffs had to pay foi machines that were brought in for the purpose of helping to reduce the high cost oi living for the people of Canada. Mr. Bain was so successful in getting these tractors into the country at a reduced rate, that he also obtained the Ottawa agency for another concern, the International Harvester Company, and it is reported brought in several hundred machines which were sold to the farmers of the West at a price of $2,200. He brought in tractors that were valued at $1,400 and sold them to the users of such machinery at $2,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to be complaining that the $2,200 tractors came in free?

What I am referring to is that tractors were brought in at a valuation of $1,400 and sold to the farmers at $2,200 and $2,400, a spread of $800 in the one case, and $1,000 in the other. My contention is that the farmers should have got the advantage of the low priced tractor as they did in the case of the 8-16 and the 10-20 tractors. In the case of the 10-20 tractors the duty was refunded to the farmers, because the Government saw the wisdom of having that duty removed. But in this case the Canadian manufacturer was deprived of the sale of the 15-30 tractor, the treasury of Canada was beaten out of their duty, and the producers of foodstuffs were obliged to pay a much higher price than they should1 have paid. That- is what I am objecting to. I am not in favour of high protection to manufacturers of agricultural implements. I stand here to-day to advocate the cause of the consumers of this country as well as the producer. The policy under which the producers get the needed facilities to produce foodstuffs that are so badly required by the plain people of this country is the policy w'hich meets with my approval and will result in more support to the Government if they will only adopt it.
Now so far as this question of tractors is concerned, let. me make myself perfectly clear. If there was nothing wrong going on in connection with the importation of these machines, why did the Advance Rumely Company have to employ Mr. John
Bain to intercede with the Commissioner of Customs, and why did the International Harvester Company have to do the same thing? When the Customs Department found out that, to use a slang expression, "the fat was in the fire," when they found out that they were discovered, an order went out from the Commissioner of Customs stating that if the size of tractor in question was being used for anything else than the production of foodstuffs duty would have to be collected amounting to between $400 and $500. I bring the minister's attention to these facts because in all probability he does not know what is going on in some departments of the Government. The President of the Privy Council has found fault with the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) in connection with food production, but if he had looked around among their colleagues he -would have found stronger reasons for complaint in that quarter than he did in the case of the hon. member for Marquette who voluntarily withdrew from the Government and threw up a large salary in order to act as his conscience dictated and in what he considered the best interests of Canada.
I wish to draw the attention of the Government to this fact, because, Sir, if ever there was a time when I believe that the Government should exert every effort to pacify the dissatisfaction that exists throughout the land, if ever there was a time when we needed a campaign to produce more foodstuffs so that the people will not be held up as they are being held up at present, it is now. And I want to say with all seriousness that it is for that purpose I am making these statements, and I am glad that the Minister of Finance is in his seat, because I hope he will endeavour to take what action he can to give to the consumers of this country as cheap foodstuffs as possible, and extract from the corporations, trusts, and combines of this land the unfair profits which they made when our boys were overseas fighting for the defence of the country and of the industries from which they have rolled up such great riches. I would ask him to do now what we were told the Government intended to do before the last election-extract from the profiteers those unfair profits, conscript them and bring them into the treasury, and so have a contented people instead of the dissatisfaction which is existing from one end of Canada to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved

by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) gives me the opportunity of saying a few words further on the matters dealt with in the Budget and the debate which has ensued thereon. I have listened with some interest and attention to the hon. member who has preceded me (Mr. Mc-Coig). He has a remarkable faculty of working himself up into a fairly well simulated state of excitement when dealing with matters which he desires to place prominently before the country. There is one aspect of his speech which rather pleased me; he appears now to be in favour of conscription.
Mr. Speaker, may I inform the hon. gentleman that I supported conscription?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, there were two or three ways of supporting conscription. My hon. friend supported it in one sense, and in another he did not. The support of conscription was the principle which divided the parties of this country at the last general election. The support of conscription was the basis upon which this Union party was founded, and upon which it will endure. My hon. friend has spoken as if the Government had taken no action whatever in obtaining a share of the profits made during the war. I have under my hand a statement, Mr. Speaker, which shows that the Government under the Business Profits War Tax has levied assessments totalling no less than $79,000,000 during the three and a half years that the tax has been in operation. During the first three years some $66,000,000 was collected in cash on assessments aggregating $72,000,000, and since that time some $7,000,000 more of business profits assessments have been made. And I desire to say this, too, because the matter is frequently overlooked in this country, that there is not in operation in any other country to-day a more severe business profits tax than our own.
Mr. MoCOIG: Maybe there is no other country where the corporations got so much money out of the people as they did in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not agree at all with my hon. friend. All over the world, during the war-in free trade England, in Canada, and. in United States, and in all the other producing countries-large profits have been made by productive enterprises. That was inevitable. The British Government imposed a business profits war tax;

so did this country; so did United States. And, so far as I know, this is the only country that is continuing its business profits war tax in its fullness this year, because I regard this ,as a war year. I want this House and the people of this country to know that we have imposed as severe a business profits war tax as any other country in the world, and that we are continuing it this year. Evidence is being continually given before the committee which is sitting on this question of profits. A large share of these profits come into the Dominion treasury. When my hon. friend accuses the Government of being derelict in collecting the business profits assessments, all I have to say is that he does not understand the situation, because I would not like to accuse him of misrepresentation.
My hon. friend, I have no doubt, will support the amendment. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had proposed to intervene in this debate for the purpose of dealing with a number of matters which have been discussed, relating principally to the financial administration of the country. On the whole, the debate has been conducted in a very moderate tone, and, with some exceptions, has been entirely free from political animus. I think it has been generally realized by the members of the House that the responsibilities of a Finance Minister during a war of the magnitude of that through which we have just passed are great indeed. War is insatiable in its demands upon the man power, the money, and the other material resources of the country. During a war the Government and the Minister of Finance, as its adviser, have really comparatively small control over the finances, because of the enormous demands made upon them-demands which cannot be gainsaid and which must be met promptly. In the Department of Finance it is not possible to equivocate or to evade responsibility; no excuse can be taken; the money must be found, whether it is $10,000,000, $50,000,000,	$100,000,000 or $500,000,000.
There is no place in which the war expresses itself so markedly from time to time as it does in the treasury of a country at war.
Among the aspects of our finance which have been subject to criticism in this House is that of the national debt of Canada. I endeavoured to make a fair, frank, and absolutely honest statement to this House and to the people as to the present financial position of the country, and as I estimated the position would be at the end of the present fiscal year when demobilization would be complete. The national debt of Canada, will be, in round figures, $2,000,000,000 at the end of the present fiscal year. It has been suggested by one or piore in the House that
4 p.m. the Government is to a certain extent responsible for the size of this national debt and for the extensive borrowing that we have done. I am sure that is not the opinion of the majority of those present in this Chamber. It was
:;008



regard to finance during the war, and I must say that on the whole they have been fairly reasonable, but when listening to some of the charges made against the Administration in respect to our finance, I could not help reflecting that the parties making those charges had but a very dim perception indeed of the immense responsibilities devolving upon us and the task which was ours in this country of finding hundreds, yes billions, as we did, of dollars for the conduct of this war. I am sorry I was not in the House last year when certain criticisms were levelled against me with regard to our Victory Loan financing, but as the matter has been brought up again this year I desire the ear of the House for a moment while I speak of the financing of this country during the war, of the responsibilities which devolved upon us and the way in which they were met, and, 1 submit, most creditably met, by this Administration.
Before the w'ar, Canada had never had a loan of $5,000,000 floated within its borders. The great money centres of the world were London, Paris and New York. If money was wanted in this country foi railway or other development, loans were floated in London or United States, and similarly with regard to the borrowings of the Federal Government and of the provincial and municipal governments. This country was not an investing country at all. The people of Canada deposited their money in the banks, and that money was let out for the purposes of trade and commerce. On the one side of the balance sheet were the deposits of the people, and on the other side the discounts and investments into which they had gone. Anything more unfair than to contrast the financing of this country with the financing, say, of United States or Great Britain during the war, can hardly be imagined. Our task was to raise not $5,000,000, but every year hundreds of millions of dollars. We had to raise more, Mr. Speaker, than the amount required for our own war expenditure, because we had to finance Great Britain in the purchase of foodstuffs raised by the people of this country. We had to finance the salmon of the Pacific coast; we had to finance the shipbuilding on the Pacific coast; we had to assist in financing the grain raised in the Canadian Northwest; we had to finance the munitions, the shipbuilding, the bacon and other food products of Central Canada, and similarly right on down to the Atlantic coast. We had to provide millions-tens

and hundreds of millions of dollars

for that purpose. These were the burdens devolving upon the Minister of Finance and the Government during the war, and I put them forward strongly because I believe that this House and the country has not appreciated the magnitude, relatively speaking, of the task that devolved upon us in raising the money, we did. 'Some hon. gentlemen not long ago said: You should not borrow. Well, if you can carry on a war without borrowing I know I should be glad to do it. Not borrow? Why, Great Britain to-day has put on a loan of five billion dollars and as much more as she can get. United States has floated a Victory Loan since the war, and she will need more money still because this is a war year.
Now we come to the question of the issues of securities, and the prices obtained for them. Canada is situated right alongside United States. Our people, invest in their markets, and they invest in ours. There is a very close connection, indeed, between the relative values of securities. What had we to contend with during the war? Great Britain at the outset of the war, in addition to sending hundreds of millions of dollars of gold to United States and selling three or four thousand million dollars' worth of securities upon the New York exchange, pledged her credit to the hilt in that country in order to obtain the money necessary to enable her to purchase on this continent the munitions, explosives, and other supplies required by herself and the Allies. To do that, she had to make continuous, issues in New York, and she put them out one after the other right to the limit before United States caane into the war. The Anglo-French loan, a five per cent loan, was put out, I think, in 1916, at 98. It went steadily down on the market until it reached as low as 89. In other words, British-French securities, that is, securities backed by the joint credit of Great Britain and France, were selling in the darkest days of the war, at the time when we had to sell our first Victory Loan here, at a price to make them yield 7 or 8 per cent, and several hon. members who have criticised our loans in this House know it, and know it very well, as 1 know. The people of this country were buying Anglo-French and other securities in New York to yield 6 and 7 and 8 per cent, and when we put our loans on, I do not say that that was a decisive factor, but it was undoubtedly a factor in the situation.
The criticisms that have been made of the cost of our loans as compared with those of United States have often been

answered. Let us consider for a moment. Here is a country as large as United States -larger geographically than United States. United States has a dense population, with great centres like New York and Chicago, where you can get subscriptions of $50,000,000 and even $100,000,000 as compared with the maximum of $5,000,000 or possibly $10,000,000 that we would get in this country. We had to cover this whole country from the Atlantic to the Pacific with our organization, and I say-not boastingly, but as a matter of fact, that cannot be contradicted-that of all the loans that weie floated during the war by any of the belligerents the last Victory Loan of Canada was by far the greatest success. How do I prove that? I think I will prove it to the satisfaction of every hon. member in this House. We raised $690,000,000 which we needed for obligations incurred, which we needed to support the men at the front and to finance Great Britain in respect of her purchases here. The population of United States is fourteen times as great as that of Canada, and her wealth at least twenty-live times as great, and I think more. A Victory Loan of $690,000,000 in Canada w7ould have as its equivalent in United States a loan of at least 15 billion dollars. Was there ever such a loan as 15 billion dollars floated in United States?
The rate of interest was different.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that; I will deal with all these matters. I said that the equivalent, in United States would be a loan of at least 15 billion dollars. The same can be said with regard to Great Britain, where the wealth is so much greater in proportion to the population as compared with this country. My hon. friend has contrasted the expense of the American loan with ours, [DOT]But I want to ask my hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Kennedy) whether he is sure he got all the cost of the American loan. I do not think he did. I want to say to the hon. member who mentioned Detroit and some other American cities in comparison with our result, that if I had put on a purely voluntary loan in this country and organized it in the way they did in United States I would have got just the same amount relatively as they got and no more. I want to point out to him the difference between the two loans, and I have the figures here in such form that every one will see the situation at a glance and will understand that this countrv,
229J
under the system we adopted in order tbs secure the money which we were obliged to have, put forth a very much greater proportionate effort, and that our system was. very much more effectual, than that of [DOT] United States. Last year when I was in ' Los Angeles, a city about the size cf Toronto-' or possibly larger and with greater wealth', they were talking there, and I could quite understand it, of the great success they had had in subscribing $30,000,000 to the Liberty Loan, and I rejoiced that they had subscribed it. But the city of Toronto, about the same size, in connection with our Victory Loan just about the same time turned' in $80,000,000, and in the last Victory Loan the city of Toronto alone turned in $140,000,000. There never was a more effectual organization got together in the. history of the world than that which we had in this country in connection with the Victory Loan, and I desire to thank every hon. member of the House and every man in the country, Liberal and Conservative alike, who helped me and helped the Government in connection with this loan, and I asked all their help. I asked the press, no matter what their political affiliations were, and the press responded.
With regard to the press-there has been some talk in the House about our expenditures for advertising in the Canadian newspapers. I wish to say that there never was a body of men anywhere who gave themselves more devotedly to effect the success of any undertaking than did the journalists of Canada in connection with our Victory Loans.
Some hon. MEMBERS.- Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The advertisingin the newspapers was placed absolutely fairly through the Canadian Press Association. I did not place it, and there was no percentage in connection with it. The cost of advertising represented only a tithe-indeed, not a tithe-of the advertising value given by the press throughout this country in promoting the success of the Victory Loan. It was not only the advertising that we paid for that was of value, but the editorial goodwill and effort of the press, which was beyond price, and I want to pay my tribute to the press for their splendid support in connection with the Victory Loan.
I called together the French-Canadian press in the city of Montreal and talked with them about the Victory Loan, and I found them a fine lot of fellows.
Were you surprised?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all. We had a beautiful evening and they rallied to the support of the Government and promoted [DOT]the success of the Victory Loan in Quebec, and we got a very much greater result than the year before. The point I want to make is that we had all elements of the community working for us.
Now we come to the question of brokers and canvassers. I called together, before the Victory Loan campaign of last fall, all the people who had acted in an executive capacity in connection with the preceding loan. They represented some of the best men in the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. There were some brokers, but the majority of those men present were business and professional men who had taken an interest in the loan the year before. We considered every aspect of the -question whether in a country like Canada we could put on a purely voluntary loan, and they said, "Yes, you can''-and I quite agreed with them-"but you will get only about half the amount of money you will obtain if you put it on in that way." We had to have the money. The war was making its enormous demands upon the country; we had a vast army overseas, and the credits that we required had to be provided from day to day. We simply had to have the money-seven hundred million dollars, if we could get it. We could have got half the amount if we had a voluntary organization such as they had in United States. Let us make some comparisons. Toronto raised $321 per capita as compared with the following amounts raised in larger American cities: St. Louis ( with a larger population), $115 per head; Boston, $202 a head; Detroit, $129 a head; Cleveland, $225 a head; Buffalo, $144 a head. Now, if I had to get the money-as I did get it-am I to be diverted from my purpose in a time of war because, in a country as vast as Canada, I have to engage canvassers to go and work night and day for three or four weeks for the two or three hundred dollars apiece which they received? Are we to be diverted from our course for such a reason? I think not. The main purpose was to get the money. The country raised the money, and the machinery that we devised was the best that could have been devised for the purpose. I could show the House telegram after telegram, letter after letter, from the Canadian Northwest and other parts of Canada pointing out that they could not get people, owing among other things to the shortage of help, IMr. Jacobs ]
to undertake the work for the commission that was offered. After all is said and done, what is five million dollars, the cost of the loan, in comparison with six hundred and ninety million dollars? What percentage is that? It is less than three-quarters of one per cent, and there never was a loan floated by the Canadian Government before the war that did not cost two per cent. I do not say that that is a fair comparison. I am only pointing out the fact that loans cost money to float and you must have regard to the extent of your country. You must have regard to the financial resources and the extent to which help is available. Between voluntary help and other help we got of a professional character, in addition to that of the canvassers, we put through one of the greatest loans that were ever floated in the world. Indeed, I believe it was the greatest, and it was put through at a time when the money had to be provided- Winnipeg raised $159 per capita and Montreal $195 per capita. Compare Winnipeg's per capita of $159 with the results in seven American cities, all larger: S't. Louis, $115, Detroit $129, Buffalo $144, Los Angeles $152, St. Paul (right across the border) $64, Seattle $124, Portland $94. Further, in the midst of our campaign we had to contend with influenza all over this country. I went wes't and when I got to Vancouver I had to cancel all eastern engagements because of the epidemic which was prevailing throughout the country, and yet we did it.
Now we come to the question of financial houses. Great Britain and Australia allow commission to financial houses in connection with their loans. Great Britain allows i, and that i is much larger than I or | here, by reason of the size of Britain's subscriptions. Why do they allow commissions to financial houses? Because it is the business of these houses to advise people . as to their investments. Figures have been put forward in this House to show that some firms received $50,000. The hon. member who gave the figures knows that there are financial houses in the country whose running expenses amount to $250,000 and $300,000 a year. Does the hon. gentleman know that last year we started in with the financial houses in August to get ready for the loan in October, and that they worked week after week and month after month and did not finish their work for months after the loan was concluded? As I say, I cannot pay too high a tribute to every one who had to do with the success of that loan. How did we determine their

remuneration? One of the best financial men in Canada is Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, and I desire to thank him for the services he has rendered me gratuitously during the war from a high sense of patriotic duty. Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, Finance Commissioner of Toronto, is one of the ablest officials in Canada and is well known to many members of this House, and an absolutely disinterested man. There is no man who speaks with greater authority upon matters of municipal and governmental finance than Mr. Bradshaw. In order that the Dominion treasury might be absolutely protected, I chose him to review the remuneration paid to financial houses in this country for the first Victory Loan of 1917, and last year I constituted a committee consisting of Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, Mr. R J. Dilworth, one of the leading accountants of the city of Toronto, and Mr. John W. Ross, of Montreal, and no better committee could have been formed than of these men. I asked them to pronounce upon the amount of remuneration that should be paid to these houses. The arrangement that I had with the latter was:	" You get your
operating expenses to the extent that you are engaged in this work." These three men went over the accounts of the last Victory Loan and they determined, from an examination of books and documents, the amount which should be paid to the firms for giving their time, and their professional services to the loan.
Mr. Bradshaw wrote me a letter on April 13, 1918, in which he stated:
The basis of remuneration to the various firms and individuals, whose services had been engaged, received careful consideration. No commission whatever was paid to them. An endeavour was made to determine emolument according to services rendered, results produced, and responsibility undertaken.
That was in connection with the loan of 1917, but in connection with last year's loan we got it down to the basis of their operating expenses, and I do not know any fairer way of dealing with it. The result is we got the organized ability and the great placing power of all the financial firms, of all the securities firms, in Canada as well as the voluntary organization which was built up throughout the country. Mr. Bradshaw points out in connection with the first Victory Loan campaign:
The time occupied in preparing for the campaign was more than twice that of any previous one. The duration of the offering wae also greater than preceding flotations, and even after the time of receiving subscriptions, the members of practically all the committees were engaged for several months in making adjustments.
Investment houses were practically prohibited from engaging in any other business during the last three months of the year. Prior to the offering, those engaged were fully occupied in organizing districts in selecting, training, and supervising the thousands of canvassers who took part.
Why, we had an army of 12,000 men working for us throughout the whole oi Canada in connection with the last Victory Loan. A country which is larger in area than United States had to be covered, and the results obtained justified absolutely the machinery we employed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to what the hon. member said about rates of interest. He asked what about United States, what about Great Britain? Does the hon. gentleman not know that American securities sold, before the war, on a one and-a-half and two per cent basis? Does he not know that in Great Britain securities were sold on a three and-a-quarter or a three and-a-half per cent basis? Have they.been able to maintain that? What rate did we pay in Canada? We had to pay over a four per cent rate when the London market was open and we were on the trustee list there. What has Great Britain had to pay for interest? The British Chancellor of the Exchequer has been subjected to a fierce attack by some newspapers because he is putting out a fifty-year loan at five per cent. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is floating a $5,000,000,000 loan and he has got to get the money. It is right to face your interest rates and to get your money. That is what he is doing. A loan for fifty years at five per cent for Great Britain, and bfefore the war the interest rate was three and-a-quarter or three and-a-half per cent! In United States, interest rates have gone up from a basis of less than two* per cent to four and-a-quarter per cent. Suppose United States had started in at the beginning of the war and had put out loan after loan as we put them out during four years? What rate of interest would she have been paying in 1918? Is it fair to compare this little country, that neveT borrowed, or was not able to borrow $5,000,000 within its own borders, with the-great opulent United States which experienced two and-a-half years of the most unexampled prosperity before it entered the war, and then to compare our rate of interest at the end of the war with the rate of interest that that great nation is paying? Do we grasp in this House the magnitude of the effort we have made in this war? We raised 50*0,000 men, and if United States had been in the war from the beginning and put up man for man with us

in proportion to population-and I have the greatest admiration for the efforts which she made for the time she was in the war -it would have meant an army of seven millions of Americans. And if United States had been in the war for four years and had raised proportionately the money that this country has raised in proportion to her wealth, which is at least twenty-five and I think more times as great as that of Canada, the United States' debt to-day instead of $25,000,000,000 would have been fifty, sixty, or seventy billion dollars at least. Now, I find no fault with United States; it made a splendid effort in the war -a wonderful effort. Bearing in mind the way that country enforced conscription, called its men to the colours and placed them overseas, and the splendid work performed over there I yield to no man in admiration for what United States has done. The only reason I put forward this comparison, is to show how unfair it is to contrast the rates of interest which this country had to pay, or the loans which it had to put out, with the rates of interest at which United States, and Great Britain were able to float their loans. We had to do the best we could, and if there is any criticism coming to this Government on the financial side, it is the criticism based on what an hon. gentleman advanced the other day-a principle to which neither I nor any man on this side of the House subscribe-that Canada had an unreasonable participation in this war. Whatever we did financially, and we did not count the money cost, we did because we were at war, because this country being in the war the people of Canada required the Government to put- forth the utmost effort as to man power and as to money power. We did that, and if there is any criticism coming to the Government for its financing during the war, that criticism is due to the fact that we participated to the extent that we did in the war, and for no other sound reason.
Now as to tax exempt bonds. One would think there had never been any tax exempt bonds in the world before. The United States securities prior to the war were tax exempt. A very considerable part of issues which have been put out since, amounting to billions of dollais, are partially tax exempt. The state and the municipal securities of the United States were tax exempt. I had an estimate made up some time last fall which shows that some $13,000,000,000 of American securities, to some degree at least, were exempt. Now I

say this: A sharply graded income tax is to a certain extent inconsistent with tax exemption. When you put out tax exempt issues you justify it on two grounds in war time; no one would ever think of putting it out in ordinary times. In the first place, your rates of interest are going up and you have to offer special inducements to the people of the country in order to get the greatest possible return. Now it is easy to say "you should not have made your bonds tax exempt." I want to say to the House, and I think I know because I discussed this question with financial institutions and with other people who know the investment situation very well, that if the last Victory Loan issue had not been tax exempt we should not have obtained anything like the amount of money we did obtain, or we should have had to pay a much higher rate of interest, and I will show you how that works out.
In United States a tax exempt bond will sell on a 1 per cent interest basis lower than a taxable bond. Supposing we had paid 6 per cent, instead of 51 -per cent last year, supposing we .had paid only one-half of one per cent more during the war, how much would we have had to pay in annual interest on $1,500,000,000? About $7,000,000 or $8,000,000. Now, it may be that it would have- been worth while to pay that in order not to have any discontent by reason of the fact that parties can buy tax exempt bonds and get certain exemption from income taxation in respect of them. But from the purely financial standpoint I have not any hesitation in saying that if you regard what you would have had to pay in additional interest, and take that excess amount of interest and apply it on the whole volume of your securities outstanding, so far as our national Budgets are concerned they will be in a better position than they would be if the bonds had been floated at a higher rate of interest and subject to taxation.
One of the ablest public men and one of the most practical minded men in this country said to me after the last Victory loan, "You will incur some criticism by reason of your bonds being non-taxable, but I wish to say to you that although income taxation anomalies will arise, you would have got just one-half the amount of money you did if your bonds had been taxable, because there would be no certainty about the rate of interest." I do not say that the people of this country would not have subscribed, but we wanted all the available money in the country for

the war. Financial institutions and wealthy individuals would say, ''We will subscribe, and subscribe well, for bonds, no matter what the interest rate is." But at the same time they would take a large part of their money and invest it in other securities which would yield a higher interest. And there was no difficulty during the war in getting a higher interest-my hon. friend from Essex (Mr. Kennedy) well knows that you could get 7 and 8 per cent upon the highest class of securities, and our people bought them freely in New York. So it got down to this question: In order to get money for carrying on the war, which was everything to the people of this country, are you going to make your bonds attractive and devise machinery which will make your loans a success-because you could not afford to have anything else but a success?
The answer is that the Government was in the war to the hilt, and we did whatever things had to be done in order to meet the situation and provide the money that would back our men up at the front and bring them back victorious and keep the credits going that would enable this country to continue the war. That is what we did, and that is what we stand on before this House and the country and what we will stand on before posterity.
Why, Mr. (Speaker, I was in continual competition in New York with the high rate of interest paid by Great Britain and the other allied countries. We put out issues in New York in 1915, and in the spring of 1917, and these securities of ours were selling down there at one time to yield 7 or 8 per cent. I want this House to know that there were pretty heavy duties and responsibilities upon this Government in connection with its finance during the war, and I am sure that most members do appreciate that fact.
Now I want to take up a few other matters. It has been stated that we should have issued our securities so that we could call them in. Well, that is not a bad principle in ordinary times. But does anybody in this House think that the Dominion Government is likely, within a few years, to be able to call in any considerable portion of the hundreds of millions of our securities outstanding? Why, we have got to raise a big Victory Loan this fall. The best feature of our finance, and the feature which has commended itself to the greatest financiers in New York and in London, is that our debt is so well funded, and the country will have time to recover,
to find the interest and to take care of the bonds as they mature. As I said during my Budget speech, if any Minister of Finance had to face the condition of our debt falling due within five years, I do not know what he would do; but it is spread over the next fifteen _ or twenty years, and well-spread. I pointed out a little while ago that Great Britain is putting out a 5 per cent loan that she cannot call in for fifty years. The British Government are facing the situation, for the same reason that we faced it; we faced it in order to get the money.
Hon. gentlemen have said, " Why, your bonds are at a premium." Well, I do not know how hon. members feel about it, but I am glad that our bonds are at a premium. I want to say that there are two million holders in this country of our war loans. If some people are buying on the exchanges to-day, they are paying a premium to the people who put up the money in the first instance. But does any hon. gentleman imagine because the bonds are at a slight premium on the market that it is any criticism of the rate at which we issued them? Give me $25,000,000 worth of bonds, and I will sell them below par in Toronto and Montreal. Anybody who knows anything about finance knows that when you come to consider putting out a Dominion loan in London you cannot put it out at the nominal market quotation, you have got . to put it out two or three points below. When our securities were at par in England, and we wanted £5,000,000, we did not put the loan out at par, we had to put it out at 97 or 98, two or three points below. Our problem was to sell $700,000,000 of securities in this country, and afterwards we devised machinery that commanded the admiration of Washington and London for stabilizing our securities during the war, and holding them up so that people, and especially the small subscribers, could sell their securities at par, at the price they paid the Government. It was a great achievement. It is a lot better that the people of this country-and all the people practically were participants in the loans- should be able to realize their bonds, ii they want to, at par, than have to sell them at four or five points discount and blame the Government for not having treated them fairly. Treat the people fairly in regard to interest rates, give them a fair deal, and they will stand by you. You may ask the people once to take your bonds below the market price, you may ask them twice, and even three times, but there comes
