a time when they will say, "We have lost a good deal of money on those bonds and we do not think we will invest in them again." Whereas, if your bonds stand at par or at a premium, why, they say, "Oh, well, here comes the Dominion Government again. Those bonds are good, and here is my money, Mr. Finance Minister, for your bonds." That is pretty good business. Treat the people fairly in regard to interest rates as well as everything else, and they will stand by you. Sometimes they will stand by you if you do not treat them fairly, but I do not believe that is a good position for a Government to take.
There is some talk about income taxation. Hon. gentlemen this morning stated that our income tax was less than that in United States. I desire to say that income tax of United States for 1918 was on a higher basis than for 1919. In other words, when the war came to an end they decreased the income tax, and I believe that our income tax to-day is on juDt about the same basis as that of United States. We aimed to make it precisely the same, and I believe it is; at least, I am so advised. Now, there is a reason for that. This country, Mr. Speaker, is inviting people to come in as immigrants and as business men. We can only meet our national debt by developing this country. We want immigration of the right kind to fill the great spaces in the West and to touch agriculture into activity which will result in great national wealth,
We desire that capital shall come in here for the development of our mineral, timber and other resources*. If you have too heavy an income tax or business profits tax you will, of a certainty, debar many people from coming into Canada.
On account of our political system being that of a federation, we have three sets of income tax. You have a municipal income tax in many provinces-for example, in Ontario; you have provincial income tax as well as municipal income tax in some provinces-for example, in British Columbia; and you have super-added to that a federal income tax. Now, the Provincial Governments are considering ways and means, just as we are. At the conference of provincial representatives that was held here last fall, if there was anything that impressed me it was the representations of Provincial Governments as to the difficulty of arranging their Budgets. They would like to have the Dominion Government increase the subsidies paid to the provinces; and the representations made to me by representatives of the provinces who attended that conference

were, without exception: "Do not invade our field of taxation more than you can help. If you increase your income tax to a very high figure, then we cannot raise the revenues which we need for all the purposes of our provinces, including education." Many of them besought me not to touch the inheritance tax, because they wanted it for their own purposes. It has been pointed out to me by many people that if the Dominion Government greatly increases the income tax or adds to the taxation already imposed upon estates by the provinces-and it may have to be done-the flow of money to charitable and educational institutions will be stopped. If, therefore, we are wise, we must have regard to provincial and municipal requirements. If any one thinks mat income taxation in this country is not high, let him take the municipal tax of British Columbia, add to that the sharply graduated income tax of that province, and add to that again the federal income tax; he will surely be satisfied, though he be the most extreme advocate of income taxation in this House, that in Canada there is a good deal of income taxation at the present time.
One word with regard to income tax collection. How long did it take United States to get a perfect system of income tax collection. It took Great Britain many years, as the member for Red Deer (Dr. Michael Clark) well knows. Great Britain has an almost perfect system, but it took seventy-five years to develop it. United States has had income tax for ten or eleven years. For the first four or five years they were not able to perfect their organization; even now their organization is not as adequate as that of England. Here we have a country stretching from Halifax to Prince Rupert, comprising cities, towns, villages, and country-side, which our income tax administration must cover. We have organizations in all the provinces. I do not want to magnify the difficulties, but I want to tell the House briefly of some of' the problems with which are confronted. As of June 16, 1919 we made 46,000 approved assessments, aggregating $11,000,000. Of these assessments, 38,000 are paid and about 5,000, or 12 per cent, of the assessments are overdue. That touches one of the features of income tax that, I think, might be dwelt upon a little. A member of this House, who was an extreme anti-tariff man, came into my office one day-he is not a member now.
I said to him, rather jokingly, " I can make you a tariff man in a week." He said "how?" and I replied, "By making you Minister of Finance." I took him over to

the register where every day is recorded the amounts that come in from the customs houses of Canada. Now, I am not putting up a plea for a high tariff; I am simply mentioning the difference between the modes of collecting these two taxes. The collection of income tax is, in the first place, inquisitorial; it goes into the affairs of every one so far as that can be done-although it is pretty difficult to go into them. Hon. gentlemen may think that it is easy to arrive at the amount of income assessment, let us say, of a farmer. Well, in some cases it is, hut very many difficulties have to be taken into consideration. For instance, what was the amount of his grain and other products last year? What is the keep of himself and his family worth? What is his farm worth and what interest should be allowed upon it as capital? What about depreciation, and all these other things? Is it, then, an easy task? I do not say that because it is not easy the Government is to be excused for not efficiently administering the Income Tax Act, but I do say that it will take two or three years, as it has in every other country, to get anything like a perfect organization of the income tax administration. That is not unreasonable; it is bound to be so. We have an organization extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific; that organization is continually being added to, and will, I believe, continue to get more efficient. I realize the soundness of the principle underlying income tax-that those who have shall pay in proportion to their means. What I am dwelling upon now is the difficulty experienced by every country in getting an efficient system of income tax administration. I assure the House that we have done the best we could in that connection and that I look forward to continued improvement.
Mr. LEMilEUX: What about large families?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an allowance now in the income tax legislation of, I think, $200 each for children under sixteen years of age.
I have made some inquiries about land tax, the alleged merits of which have been put forward in the House. I remember reading years ago with the greatest pleasure Mr. Henry George's exposition of the theory of land taxation. He pointed out- what I knew, because I had charge of assessments in Toronto-the absolute impossibility of getting at income tax assessment and personal property assessment as
it should be got at. He pointed out that the assessment should be upon the land,, because the land could be seen. I am not endorsing the theory; I am merely informing the House what his views were with regard to income and personal property taxation and pointing out that Mr. George contended that land taxation was the only taxation that should be resorted to. I have given the matter a good deal of consideration and have discussed it with provincial treasurers and representatives of Provincial Governments. It was impressed upon me that to impose a federal land tax on top of the municipal and provincial land taxes would create a rather serious situation, especially in the West. I do not know how serious it would be, but I do not find any widespread public opinion in favour of a land tax. I am speaking now of a tax upon all land, in cities, towns, and villages, and throughout the country. I am told that some provinces of the West have a wild lands tax.
Land taxation lies immediately at hand so far as the municipality in the province is concerned. I do not mean to commit myself here to the principle that the Dominion Government will not at any time resort to an estate tax or to a land tax. I am simply dealing with the present situation and pointing out that we have carefully canvassed these matters, and I am giving some of the reasons why it does not appear advisable for the present at least to introduce such taxation as has been mentioned.
Has the minister any idea what a land tax would yield?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I estimated it once and I was disappointed- I think at as high a rate as four mills-I am speaking only from memory-it would not exceed $20,000,000, which, of course, is a substantial amount, but nevertheless I was surprised at the comparatively small amount, as it seemed to me, that would be raised by a four-mill rate.
We have been attacked with regard to our expenditures since the war and with regard to credits that we have extended. The Government have felt a very heavy sense of responsibility with regard to expenditures which we are making this year, and if we felt we could have refrained from making the expenditures we have made, we should have been glad. I pointed out to the House on one or two occasions during the session the situation with which we were confronted immediately after the

signing of the armistice-hundreds of thousands of people about to be thrown out of work in our cities, soldiers returning to the extent of over 300,000 in a period of a few months-and they are coming back by tens of thousands now. That is the situation with which the Government was confronted, and we have not hesitated to spend money, nor have the British authorities. If you look at the expenditure of Great Britain, you will find this is a war year in that country. The British authorities are paying out tens of millions of dollars to men in unemployment; their expenses are colossal; they are facing the situation that resulted by reason of the profound dislocation caused by the war. Society has been torn' almost to pieces; men were 'taken from their ordinary pursuits which were filled by others; they were taken for the war, for transportation, and all the other services connected with the war; many were placed in other industries, and society must painfully restore those men to their callings. That cannot be done in a week or a month or six months or a year. The nations of the world are to-day on a war basis as regards expenditure, and in order to keep society together in this trying period after the war we are pouring out tens of millions of dollars on shipbuilding. Why are we providing a $50,000,000 credit for the purchase of timber in British Columbia. British Columbia could not have sold her timber, and thousands of men would have been out of employment but for the $50,000,000 credit which we established for Great Britain last fall. The same is true with regard to our programme of railway extensions and all the credits we have extended abroad. I cannot forecast what the future holds, nor can any body else, but the great problem that this continent must face this next year is how to enable Europe to buy the goods which we have of agricultural and other production. That is the question that is perplexing the statesmen at Washington and the financiers in New York and us in Canada. We are going to have a great crop in the West, and we are going to have other products to the extent of probably hundreds of millions of dollars to sell, and so have the United States, only on a much vaster scale. How is Europe going to buy those? We will furnish all the credits we can and the United States Government is extending tens of millions of dollars' oi credit for purchases in that country. The financiers of New York are joining up with the Government to devise ways and means to help out the situation by private enter-
prise, and that is what we must do in this country. The sooner that private enterprise can do this, the better, and nobody will be more pleased that I shall; but if private enterprise cannot do it without governmental assistance, without joint action, then I think the Government must co-operate. This war has torn Europe to pieces. How are we going to feed Germany and Austria, our enemies as well as our Allies? If the war is going to end, how are they going to buy the millions of dollars of produce they require from this continent? How are they going to get the money in Canada and United States to buy it? Credits will have to be established. How they will be established, whether solely by Government, or jointly by Government and private interests, I do not know, but the question is one which we cannot lightly put aside. Whether we like it or not, the question will be put up to us. I have been too long in this House listening to debates to appear to instruct the House, but I have often thought that none of us, members of the Government as well as the members generally, realizes what would happen if certain action that we have taken had not been taken. Supposing, last fall, when financial arrangements for the purchase of our wheat broke down, we had. said; Well, the Government cannot find $170,000,000-and I never expected in the world to have to find it-required to buy our wheat and flour; supposing the Government had taken the advice of some hon. members and said: We will not provide it; we will leave the matter to private enterprise. Well, we would soon hear about it. The wheat would all back up; the mills would stop; commerce would at once be affected throughout the country. So long as the money is provided everything goes forward beautifully. Nobody cares particularly how the money is provided; but if that money were not provided, we would have a very serious situation in this country. As to what credits we should give, I am not prepared to say, because nobody can forecast what lies ahead this next year. I know that the world will meet the situation; I know this continent will devise ways and means necessary. If you have a town in which there are two or three solvent people who have goods other people want in order to live, and if you have a number of other people around who have no money or very little and who need those goods or they will starve, or be in want, or be cold, what happens? Credit must be given, and in the same manner this continent will have to give credit to

Europe, although I do not know what form that credit will take. I ask hon. members, in connection with any criticism they have of anything the Government is doing within reason, to bear in mind that this is an exceptional time, in this, that we must provide work in this country to the full extent of our capacity, and that we must, as a Government, or through financial agencies, find the money necessary to market our exportable products. The Government would be delighted if it did not have to do that. We are not putting on loans for the sake of putting them on, but we have to look forward to this fall and this coming winter with the men back from overseas and the high cost of living that has so often been referred to in this House, and the fact that we must get a market for our products. Those are the duties and responsibilities devolving upon the Government, and I need not assure hon. members that, at times, they are pretty heavy. I welcome criticism; nobody values it more than I do, because occasionally, indeed, frequently, you get an idea that is of service to you, and I am only too happy to acknowledge it. I have derived many suggestions in this House that have been of the greatest possible value, and I do not mean to say, looking over the past iour years, that we have not made mistakes, because we have, but we have made very few. I say that, and I do not believe anybody holds himself to a higher standard than I do.
The minister admits that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that we admit it. How many perfect people are there in the world, outside, let us say, of my hon. friend?
Two of us, perhaps.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We never claimed perfection. All that we do claim is an honest intention, fair courage and resources, and a desire to promote so far as we can the interests of the people of this country whom we represent.
Now let me say a word or two about another matter that has engaged, and properly engaged, a good deal of attention in this House, and that is the high cost o) living. There have been various angles of approach to it-a pick here, a dab there, and a dent yonder-but what are the great underlying causes? I believe that most members of this House know what they are. If all of us would just drop the politician and ask ourselves what is the cause of the high cost of everything, I think
we would have no difficulty in ascertaining what it is. Fifty million people of the greatest nations of the world have been withdrawn from their pursuits and poured into the war; tens of millions from agriculture in Europe, and millions from agriculture Overseas' What does that mean, as far as agricultural production is concerned? It means diminished production, greatly diminished production. Then what about the destruction of the war throughout Europe-the vast areas of agricultural territory destroyed, the cattle carried off oi killed, the horses taken away, the implements of agriculture broken, whole producing districts devastated ? How long is it going to take to have that agriculture flourishing again, how long is it going to take to have those herds restored ? How long is it going to take to replace that labour of tens of millions of men, replaced as it was, imperfectly and partially, by old women and children during the war? Large areas of Europe are starving. What are the two concomitants of war? Plague and famine. We had the plague, and it killed almost as many as the war, and in the world to-day we have many of the aspects of famine. We have food scarcity. Consider the amount of food destroyed in ships sunk by submarines, and the food destroyed at the Front. Consider the increased consumption of food by millions of men in the army, many of whom were fed as they had never been fed before. The standard oi living throughout the world has been raised. All those engaged in war and other industries have been consuming more than they did before the war. The demands upon food have been much greater. What do I draw from all that? In the first place we have diminished production, and in the second place increased consumption. When you have diminished production and increased consumption, what world phenomenon do you get? Scarcity of food and of all other kinds of commodities. That is the main cause of the present high prices- diminished production and greatly increased consumption. Our cities have been filled up by people who have come from the country to engage in war industries. The farmer is clamouring for help and cannot get it. The problem of this country and of all countries, and the prob lem of the trend towards the city. That problem is not confined to Canada. It is present in France, in England, in Germany, and in the United States. If anybody will look up the statistics he will be startled at what they show. That is the situation which we have.

If there are combines by all means take whatever action is necessary in order that there may be free competition, but no matter what Government is in power there will be men in Free Trade England and men in this country and in United States who for one reason or another will make large sums of money from time to time, in spite of any action that may be taken by the Government, and if that money is honestly made, it is a national advantage instead of a disadvantage. As for combines if there are any, dissolve them. I do not mean to say that in	time of
war, or if occasion should require it, there should not be food control, but the experiments that have been made in food control during the war have not been very happy. Interfere with the price of milk, for example, and cattle are killed for beef. It is the same all down the line. J made an experiment which my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. MeCrea) has always commended me for in this House, that of fixing the price of news print, and it was a very difficult task indeed.
Hon. gentlemen say that if these are the main causes of the scarcity of food and other supplies, what is the use of the committee that has been appointed by this House? I think it is a great deal of use, if for no other reason than the publicity that is given; I am a great believer in publicity. There is another thing. I think we have all got into too extravagant personal habits in this country. I went into a store not very long ago, if I may be personal for a moment, to buy a hat. A hat that cost me $4.50 before the war was offered me for $11. I said " I won't buy it, that is too much."

Was it a minister's
hat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was an English hat.
Was it a lady's hat'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You might think so from the price, but it was not a lady's hat. It was a hat my hon. friend could have worn with that dignity with which he wears all his clothes. I said I could not afford it. My own view is that we do not inquire sufficiently as to what we ought to pay; we have got into the habit of paying almost anything we are asked without inquiring whether we could buy to better advantage elsewhere. We do not bargain.
I remember years ago our wives would know where they could get a thing the cheapest. They had a wide range and did

not pay any price that was asked. If the people of this country, when the price is too high, would say "I am sorry, I cannot afford it," it would tend to bring the prices down. The committee that has been appointed can do good if they get all the facts, and they should be careful to get all the facts so that no wrong impression goes out one way or the other. If high prices are due to some speculative change in prices, let us have the facts. If it is a question of return on capital, let us have the facts. The great thing under democratic government is to get the facts and give them to the people, and that is one great thing the committee can do. In addition to that, they may discover that there are certain combinations, and if they do, I shall be most happy to help enforce sound recommendations in that respect.
I want to speak about the prospects for the future. This country, as I said when introducing the Budget, has a very heavy load of debt. All the other nations that have been engaged in the war are in the same position, only more aggravated. Europe is freighted down with debt. Now the interest on that debt is going to have its effect on prices of everything for years to come, and so far as I can see the only salvation of the world is that which has always saved it-Work, work. I do not mean to say that any man should work longer hours than will give the best results from his productive powers. I am in sympathy with the aspirations of labour for a reasonable day, but I am not speaking about labour alone. I say that all classes in the world will have to work, and work hard. After Waterloo, how was the enormous debt of England met? Any one who will take the trouble to read about it will find that it was met by the people of England making up their minds that they would produce more in order that they might live up to the standard they enjoyed before and also pay that debt. United States faced a greater debt after the 'Civil War and extinguished it practically within twenty-five years. This great producing country, if we can get the people to produce and save, can look forward with confidence to the future, and I say that without in the least degree minimizing the extent of the debt and the gravity of the problems before us. We can do it. If we cannot, what other nation in the world, in the present situation, is going to be able to do it? I reiterate, we can do it. There is just one other thing I want to say, and say with all sincerity: I think there is too much of a tendency-I will not say in

this House-to take it for granted that all persons who stayed at home were profiteers. Now, the noblest kind of service was rendered in this country by thousands of men and women from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Take our Red Cross contribution, the Patriotic Fund, and the other multitudinous enterprises in which the people at home were engaged in connection with the war. The spirit of the Canadian people was magnificent during the war. The farmers did well, the manufacturers did well, and the traders did well. My own view is that we should not have been able to carry on the war if the country as a whole had not done very well. I do not believe that men should make undue profits. I am opposed to that, but I must say that I like to see business enterprises in the country, at the beginning of a period such as that which now confronts us, in fairly good shape to keep their hands engaged and meet whatever difficulties may lie ahead. I am opposed to undue profits on the part of any one, but I like to see successful trade and its results, because we have to shoulder a heavy burden and solve the serious problems which lie before us. I believe that in the next year, two years, three years, or five years, we are going to have as keen competition as this world can produce in all lines. Why do I say that? Europe must produce and sell abroad or it cannot sustain the burdens which the war has placed upon it. So the people of Canada-and I am sure they will be able to do it-must be prepared to meet the keenest kind of competition within the next five years. I think we are in a good position 'to do it. Unrest? Yes! Unrest all over the world. It is partly psychological, due to the strain through which we have passed; and, in part, it is due, I think, to a sense of rather profound injustice on the part of many as to the way in which the war has distributed its burdens and sacrifices, and the feeling that there should be far-reaching social readjustment. All that is reasonable, and it will take time before the world can steady down after this war. I believe I said that work was necessary; another thing, I think, is also necessary, as an indispensable concomitant. I Delieve that work and the Golden Rule are going to solve many of the problems that lie before us if the people will only do the one and apply the other. Legislation? Yes! Legislation to the extent that it will accomplish justice. But it is slow and uncertain in its processes. At the basis of the dispute between capital and labour lies, in my judgment, the field of ethics. The Golden Rule,
if we would all apply it, would do a world of good. The world will never be saved by legislation alone. It will be saved by the due observance of moral principles and a proper regard for ethics; in other words, religion, although I am the last man to preach. The sooner that all the people of this country and the world over realize the righto ot others, and not only desire to respect thrrn, but carry that desire into practice in all the relations of life, the sooner will things become settled and men solve successfully the troublous problems with which they are faced to-day. The war is not yet over, and until Monday next its conclusion will be a matter of uncertainty. I do not know, and I do not believe that any one in the world knows, whether it is over, and the war may continue after 'Monday next.
So far as fiscal policy goes, it is for governments to consider situations as they arise from time to time and deal with them as wisely as they can. It was put forward this morning that we had made some reductions in the Budget as a sop to the West. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is not true. My desire in budgets has always been to take into account the country as a whole. It is idle to disguise from ourselves the fact that a large section of Western 'Canada has been disturbed on tariff matters. I do not believe that there are twenty members in this House who would seriously put forward the proposal that we should undertake in this troubled period, in view of the conditions which I have mentioned, not only domestic, but international, to tear the tariff to pieces and put it together again. I do not believe that there are twenty members who would say that we coul'd intelligently revise the Canadian customs tariff to-day. But the view is expressed that taking the duties off foodstuffs may give some relief. I think that is probably true with regard to articles that are not grown in this country- I am frank to say that I agree with the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) that in a great food producing country like this where you produce more than you need, duties upon food products have an almost imperceptible effect on prices. As regards tea, sugar and coffee, and things produced only outside of the country, there is no question that if you take the duty off you get an almost immediate result. But as regards food whidh we produce to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars more than we require, the diminution of duties would have no important effect on prices. So far'as policy is concerned I would, li&ve duties rest more
They did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They did not, and they would not if they were in power.

,Mr. McKENZIE: The Finance Minister says that the amendment of the hon. member for Brome is chaff. Will he say that the platform of the Grain Growers' Association is also chaff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not for the moment dealing with the platform of the Grain Growers' Association, but I have no hesitation in saying:-I am on record on too many occasions to have any hesitancy in the matter-I believe in a fiscal policy which tends to develop and stabilize the industries of this country, and that policy will govern me in my administration. I would so direct the policy of Government that the industries of a country would be promoted and stabilized and that taxation should bear as lightly as possible upon the people as to necessities and as much as possible upon luxuries. The platform on which I stand has been too often declared by me in this House to admit of arty misunderstanding. Above all, I would say to my hon. friend that no matter what platforms he shapes or adopts-because I do not think he has thought out yet the platform he is going to adopt-he has had two or three in the last few weeks-if he was occupying the treasury benches to-day notwithstanding the amendment for which hon. gentlemen opposite are going to vote, they would not tear the Canadian tariff to pieces at this time; they did not do that when they were in office. Look through the utterances of my predecessor, Hon. Mr. Fielding-and I have always had the greatest respect for that gentleman; no man will find that I have ever said much in criticism in this House of the former Minister of Finance-and it will be found that the Liberal Government continually had the interest of this industry and of that and the other, at heart. They established the steel industry in 'Cape Breton by bounties to which my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) subscribes. Did they refrain from imposing any particular duties on iron and steel? There were duties on iron and steel before this Government came into power. Who put them there? Let us face the facts, and it is a fact, that the Liberal Government under Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier did have regard for particular industries in this country. Therefore, I say that this amendment, designed to look like grain for the benefit of the farmer, is chaff, and will be so regarded, I believe, by the farming community of this country. There is an agitation in the West, in regard to agricultural implements, principally, and there has been for many years. The former
Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in the reciprocity agreement provided for certain reduced duties upon agricultural implements and other products of Canada. The chief objection that I had to the reciprocity agreement was the fact that there was an agreement. What have we got to-day without any agreement? Flour is on the free listj wheat is on the free list; this Government put them there. Cement is lower than it was under the reciprocity agreement. Binders are lower than they were undeT the reciprocity agreement, and the other articles dealt with in the Budget are as low, if not lower than they were under that agreement. Reference has been made to the necessities of the three Prairie Provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, feut in the tariff policy regard must be had to the country as a whole from the Atlantic to the Pacific, to the national interests as a whole. If you can meet the wishes to a certain degree, at least, of an important section of the community, without doing material damage to the national interest, you ought to do it; and this Budget- represents a sincere attempt to keep stable at this unstable time the industries of Canada, and at the same time go as far as we can to meet the legitimate requests of those interested in tariff reduction. The first thing that any Finance Minister must do is to provide money to meet the national indebtedness. Members may say: Take the tariff down. But what will be the consequence of that? How are you going to meet your debts from day to day? As I say, the amendment would cut off 150,000,000, as between revenue and current expenditure, and provides nothing to take its place.
Another thing I pointed out in my Budget speech, that the expenditures of this country on ordinary account had been doubled by the war. $100,000,000 more interest on the public debt; of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 more in two or three years for pensions; $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 on account of soldiers' re-establishment; $150,000,000 or $160,000,000 of current expenditure added to the expenditure of the Dominion before the war. How are you going to meet it? Nobody will say that you can raise it by income taxation only, or by land taxation only, or by inheritance taxation only. No, nor a fraction of it. If you put on all the taxes under those three heads that the country can stand, you would not begin to meet the expenditure. We have got, like a manly nation, to meet our obligations arising out of the war. We have got to meet the pension fund-that is the first thing we

.should meet; and we have got to meet these other charges to take care of our soldiers- and there will be more to come-to provide war gratuities to help the returned soldier bridge over the time until he gets back to the productive occupations of civil life. We have got to do all that, and we are going to do it. But if you tear the tariff to pieces at this time, or at any time for that matter, how are you going to get the money? .
I said in my Budget speech that the time was overdue for a rearrangement of the tariff. I say so still. And we have taken the necessary steps to provide for that at the proper time after an investigation has been held. But to put in effect this amendment at this time would be a fatal policy, fatal to the credit of the country by reason of the gap that it would leave between revenue and expenditure. And, further than that, if you diminish our revenue without providing other revenue to take its place to the same extent and on the same scale, you are going to make this country scrutinize too carefully the expenditures which we should incur on account of the returned soldier. Your Minister of Finance should have abounding revenues so that he can do his duty by the country in the way of maintaining its credit and meeting its obligations and the just claims of the soldiers upon the citizens of this country. In that spirit this Budget has been framed.
There is another thing most essential in this country to-day to my judgment, and that is that we should have national unity. This Dominion is broken up into four great sections. You have the Maritime Provinces; then you have a gap of a few hundred miles until you come to the city of Montreal and the more populous parts of Quebec and Ontario; then you have a great gap of a thousand miles of wilderness and you come to the three great Prairie Provinces -any one of them almost unlimited in its resources, and as large geographically as Germany or France; and then you have the Rocky mountains and beyond them the province of British Columbia. You have all these different sections with diverse sectional interests. What is going to be the policy of any Government-of this Government and of its successors? They have a large family and they cannot play favourites. You can hardly have a Benjamin-although I said once that Prince Edward Island should be the Benjamin, because it is so small geographically and is such a beautiful little province-you have to survey the whole situation and adopt a policy that will be best for Canada as a

whole, nationally speaking, and I am sure that I am voicing the sentiments of every man in this House, because they are all patriotic, when I say that they will support a policy which best accords with the national interest of Canada and all its parts. That does not mean that we cannot redress injustice if it should exist; it means the opposite of that. It does not mean that from time to time tariffs should not change to meet changing conditions. But it does mean that in considering a fiscal policy the whole of Canada must be taken into account and such a policy adopted as will promote that end, and I believe that every section of Canada-Maritime, Central and Prairie Provinces, and British Columbia-will support that policy if they understand and believe it to be a national policy, for I have the greatest confidence in the people of Canada.
I have taken up a good deal of time, Mr. Speaker, and I feel that I should the more apologize because we asked members to cut down their speeches. But I have felt very seriously the responsibilities which have devolved upon me as financial adviser of the Government during the war; I have taken them quite conscientiously, and I did desire to place upon Hansard for the information of this House and of the country, and of those coming after who might desire to inquire, the views of the Minister of Finance upon his financial administration during the war and the conditions which confront the country immediately after the war. I have felt it advisable that I should do that; and if I have taken up too much time and wearied your patience over much, I hope that for the reason given you will be inclined to extend to me reasonable indulgence.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

speakeroldname: Mr. SAMUEL WILLIAM JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is
very little which at this stage I can add to the debate which has proceeded for nearly two weeks. During the last ten or twelve days we have had in this House addresses from various members dealing with the matters mentioned in the Budget. Most of them have been illuminating, many of them have been interesting; and I do not feel that I can add anything to what has already been said. In the early part of the debate we had the heavy artillery; subsequently we had the cavalry galloping

across the ground; after that we had the machine guns in action; and now the duty devolving upon me is to do a little sniping on my own account, if I find that there is occasion therefor.
This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) was delivered of his second Budget speech. We had expected the delivery of one child, but thanks to the amendment which was introduced by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) the House has been presented with twins; and the Minister of Finance tells us that he expects these children to be "protected" and cared for by the people of this country. I have no quarrel with the Minister of Finance with regard to the excellent address he delivered this afternoon, with a good deal of which I agree. Were it not for the intense heat, I am sure we would all have enjoyed the two , hours or more which he took up in his interesting, didactic lecture to us upon the finances of this country.
The Finance Minister felt himself, if 1 may use the expression on a hot day like this, to be " skating on thin ice " in certain parts of his address. The member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) made the assertion that the Government had been robbed of large stims of money through the importation into Canada of tractors upon which the duty had not been paid, and yet that the farmer or the consumer did not receive the benefit. The minister ignored that serious charge, and went on with talk of generalities, of which he is a master.
The Finance Minister spoke about the wonderful achievement of the Government in 1914 in reducing the national debt by $5,000,000. The minister did not, however, take the trouble to enlighteen the House by stating how much money had been drawn from the people during that year. The public accounts show that in 1914 $127,384,000 were taken from the people and credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and spent. While I am on that subject, I wish to point out the wide divergence between the expenditure chargeable to consolidated fund under the Liberal Government during the years 1909, 1910, and
1911,	and that of the subsequent years,
1912,	1913, and 1914. During the last years of the Liberal administration the expenditure was $84,000,000 in 1909, $79,000,000 in 1910, and $87,000,000 in 1911, and we find that in 1912, 1913, and 1914, the figures run up to $98,000,000, $112,000,000, and $127,000,000. No wonder the Minister of Finance was able to pay off in 1914 a paltry $5,000,000 of the national debt, when he was able
to pay out on current account in that year a sum of $127,000,000.
Another criticism I have to make is that notwithstanding the present high cost ot foodstuffs, the Government has granted credits to foreign countries for the purpose of furnishing them with foodstuffs from this country, thus increasing the cost ol living. It has been trumpeted throughout the country that vast sums of money are being credited to countries on the other side of the Atlantic to enable them to purchase foodstuffs in Canada, notwithstanding the fact that we have not enough food to satisfy our own needs. It is a question whether the Government is justified in advancing money in order that foodstuffs may be shipped out of the country, because of the inability of our people to obtain in many cases the actual necessities of life, bringing about so much distress and consequent unrest.
I do not purpose to deal at length with the merits and demerits of protection and free trade, which have been so fully and thoroughly discussed in this House, on the one side by the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and on the other side by the member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). I would like to say, howe.ver, that the member for Red Deer is to be congratulated upon his address; I do not know that 1 ever heard a discourse so illuminating and so clear as that which the eloquent member from the West gave us on this subject. With some of the views that he advanced I cannot say that I am entirely in agreement. For instance, he seemed to advocate an insurgency on the part of members of a political party, looking towards complete independence of view. It seemed to me that he laboured the point, I consider that independence on the part of members of a political party, at any rate in this country, should be sparingly exercised. The member for Red Deer spoke of Cobden having been an insurgent of that class; surely he does not expect that a Cobden is to rise up every year. If we are to teach the rank and file of our party that they may at any given moment express independent views on public matters, where is this to lead? I commend to my hon. friend the remarks of that great parliamentarian and constitutionalist Sir Thomas Erskine May on the merits and demerits of party Government.
I quote the following from the remarks of that learned author:
We find that Government without party is absolutism-that rulers, without opposition, may be despots. We acknowledge, with gratitude, that we owe to party most of our rights and



liberties. We recognize in the fierce contentions of our ancestors, the conflict of great principles and the final triumph of freedom. We glory in the eloquence and noble sentiments which the rivalry of contending statesmen has inspired. We admire the courage with which power has been resisted; and the manly resolution and persistence by which popular rights have been established. We observe that, while the undue influence of the Crown has been restrained, democracy has been also held in check. We exult in the final success of men who have suffered in a good cause. We admire the generous friendships, fidelity, and self-sacrifice -akin to loyalty and patriotism,-which the honourable sentiments of party have called forth. We perceive that an opposition may often serve the country far better than a ministry ; and that where its principles ai-e right, they will prevail.
By argument and discussion truth is discovered, public opinion is expressed, and a free people are trained to self-government. We feel that party is essential to representative institutions. Every interest, principle, opinion, theory and sentiment, finds expression. The majority governs: hut the minority is never without sympathy, representation, and hope. Such being the two opposite aspects of party, who can doubt that good predominates over evil? Who can fail to recognize in party, the very life-blood of freedom?
I can understand, of course, why the hon. member for Red Deer made the plea that he did. He found himself constrained only a short time ago to stray from the flock, and this, I fancy, is his justification and apology for returning. We are, however, very glad to have the hon. member with us once more; we welcome the prodigal, and we hope the experience he has learned on the other side will serve him in good stead, and that we shall have the benefit of his advice as to what happened to him during the time he was away and since he left our . party in 1917.
The 'Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has our sympathy in his efforts to reconcile two such widely divergent groups in his party, and in his desire to satisfy both he has pleased neither. That is always the fate of people who attempt to do a work of that kind. The Minister of Finance, I suppose, is not oblivious of the story in Aesop's Fables of the man and his son who were riding an ass. The man was advised by his friends that it might be well if they both got down and that the ass should ride upon them, and (t ended that neither of the parties were satisfied and that the ass was subsequently drowned. It is necessary for public men in this country to take a firm position upon political questions and to stand or fall by their principles, but the Government are so anxious for power, they are so anxious to retain their seats on the treasury benches that they were willing to swallow themselves and to sacrifice prin-

ciple in order that they might remain where they are.
I was very much impressed by a remark which fell from the lips of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder). He said, if I remember well, that this was-no time to deal with tariff revision, and I agree with him fully and entirely in that statement. This is not the time for the Government to deal with tariff revision; this is the time for the Government to dissolve Parliament and go to the country. The Government was elected for one specific purpose, namely, to impose conscription upon the country, and as they said, to win the war. Conscription was imposed, the war is won, and it is now the duty of the Government to appeal to the country for a further lease of power. That seems to me to be the constitutional aspect of the situation, and that was the course followed by Mr. Lloyd George in 1918. Hardly was the ink dry on the armistice on November 11, 1918, when the Lloyd George Government was dissolved and went to the country. Why did not this Government do the same? Why does it persist in hanging on to power?' Why does this Government, with the divergent elements on the other side, the protectionist element, represented by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), the-free trade element which has been represented heretofore by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), and every possible element of that kind which was banded together for the purpose of imposing conscription on this country and winning the war, persist in trying to force down the throats of its followers this tariff revision which they will not have? Many hon. gentlemen opposite are actually committing [DOT]political suicide when they venture to vote for the Government as it is at present constituted. They know very well they can never come hack; indeed, it is a question in many cases if they can even go home to see their people. Yet the Government endeavours to force on them this measure upon which they have not been elected to pass. If there ever were a case when the Government ought to appeal to the people, this is the occasion, and the Government is simply holding the treasury benches for the purpose of remaining in power, because if I am any judge of events in the country at the present day, this Government when it submits itself to the people will find itself on this side of the House as soon as the people declare by their votes what their views are.
I am sure we on this side of the House sympathize with hon. members on the other

side who are being stampeded by the Government in the way in which they are. We see the surgings on their side. We know what is going on. Some of them have broken away-the strong ones. Some are debating in their minds whether they should follow the Government or whether they should vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). The weak ones have already gone over, horse, foot and artillery, expecting to have a little joy-ride as long as it lasts, because they know they can never hope to enter these halls again, inasmuch as, according to our view, they will have acted treacherously with their electors if they vote for this Budget which, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) says is nothing more nor less than a protectionist Budget. Let us take the case of the repeal of the 5 per cent, and on certain goods of the 7i per cent war tax. These war duties brought into the treasury something like $45,000,000 last year. The Minister of Finance has proclaimed in this House and throughout the country the fact that $17,000,000 of that has been taken off, leaving $28,000,000 which the people of this country will be obliged to pay in addition to the regular customs duty. Calculating that the customs duties in 1914, the first year of the war, were $100,000,000, roughly speaking-I have not the figures at hand at the moment-what does this $28,000,000 mean? It means that the people of this country are paying 28 per cent more into the treasury in the matter of import duties than they did in 1914. Yet we are told that this is a tariff revision. War duties are imposed on the people when there is no war. We have two Ministers of Militia, one an overseas minister, when there is no necessity at all for an overseas minister, seeing that our men are practically all back. We have also the Department of Agriculture not filled, and I make bold! to predict that the position will not be filled for many moons, the reason being that the Government is afraid to open any constituency where a Minister of Agriculture could submit himself for election in order to test the feeling of the people. Where is the Minister of Agriculture to come from? Naturally and logically from the West. Is there any one member on the other side coming from an agricultural district in the West who is willing to submit to the test of being elected by the people before he takes his seat as Minister of Agriculture? I predict that the Department of Agriculture will be an appendage to the Department of Immigra-2301
tion and Colonization for some time to come. The Department of Agriculture is one of the most important departments of the Government.
Would it not be well if the Minister of Militia Overseas were to take over that department? That is a suggestion which I throw out to the Government. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There again my hon. friend is not stating fairly what I said to the House. I said that the Minister of Agriculture, I believed, had done everything which he thought prudent and wise in dealing with the whole matter, that he had acted most efficiently in* the discharge of his duty. Of course, as a member of the Government, I take full responsibility with the Minister of Agriculture for all that was done in the premises.

I do not see that the President of the Privy Council could do anything else. Nothing was done, anyway. What I said was that the President of the Privy Council had made the statement that if there was any inefficiency, the blame must be laid at the door of the Minister of Agriculture. That reminds me of the old Levitical law, which my hon. friend knows very much better than I do. When sins of ignorance were committed by the people, how did they escape responsibility? They got a yearling goat and sacrificed it, and the sins of the people were placed upon its head. That is what the Government have attempted to do with the ex-Minister of Agriculture. The sins of the Government in connection with the high cost of living and the general administration of the Department of Agriculture are placed on the head of this poor goat the hon. member for Marquette, who is just a little more than a year old as a minister-a year and-a-half to be exact. I am glad to know that after all, the Levitical law can be made to apply in the year of grace 1919 as well as three thousand years ago.

Let us consider the question of customs brokers' commission for passing entries from one department of government to another. Tens of thousands of dollars went into the pockets of friends of the Government who were acting as brokers. The work they did could be done by a clerk in any of the departments receiving $700 or $800 a year, and yet for a pure matter of bookkeeping, in order to keep proper tab on the merchandise and commodities brought in for the Government from one department to another, we paid in one instance, if I remember rightly, something like $16,000 to a firm o'f brokers in Quebec. I am speaking without the figures before me, but I think it was $16,000. I say, therefore, that while we have given this money freely and gladly in order to win the war, the Government must recognize the fact that this country will hold them to strict accountability when they go before the people, for then they will be asked to explain how these vast sums of money were allowed to filter through their hands, and in many cases into the pockets of friends of the Government.

No one takes the income tax seriously in this country. It is treated as a joke. Nine-tenths of the people do not pay the tax for the excellent reason that statements are never sent to them. I know of instances where accounts were prepared and forms were

filled up, and for the last two years not one word has been heard from the department with regard to these statements of account. They run into millions of dollars, and the interest upon these sums is also [DOT]considerable. But for 3ome reason or other known to the Government, no serious effort is made to collect this money. I understand that in Australia, which has five-eighths of the population of this country, they collect in income tax something like $37,000,000. Proportionately to that, Canada ought to contribute $50,000,000 on income tax account. But how much have we collected? I understand that last year we collected the paltry sum of $6,000,000. How long is this condition going to continuer The Minister of Finance threw an interesting sidelight on this question this afternoon. He said: I told a friend of mine that I would convert him very easily to protection if he were to come into my office, because I could show him that every day large sums of money are being paid into various customs houses in the Dominion of Canada on account of imports. He further said: It is easier to collect this money and consequently we do not have to bother about the other. Now, I submit that it is unworthy of the Minister of Finance to speak in that way. It is not a question whether or not the money can be easily collected. It is a question of proportioning the taxes of the country equitably upon all the people.
The Government deserves credit for some of its legislation, and I might instance the Bankruptcy Act which went through the House and passed the Senate a few days ago. I was very glad that the Government put through that Bill. )I had the honour of introducing it myself into this House last year. This year I thought it would be more in keeping with things were the Government to take hold of an important piece of legislation of that kind and put it through, and they have done so, although they have tacked on to the Bill several anomalies for which I do not wish to hold myself responsible, and of which I disclaim the paternity. However, I have to admit that the Act was very much needed in the interests of commerce, and to that extent the Government has followed the views of the commercial community generally in putting through that Bill.
I have another Bill in my hands which I am prepared to tender to the Government. It is a Bill which has been standing in my name for the last two or three months. It had not reached the Committee stage

when private members' day was taken by the Government and consequently I was unable to proceed with it further. May I suggest to my hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that this Bill is almost identical in form with one which he introduced into this House on January 16, 1908. On reference to Hansard, page 1346, I see:
Mr. R. L. Borden (Oarleton, Ont.) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 66) to amend the House of Commons Act. He said:	This Bill
has the same purpose as a Bill introduced last session or the session before. It is to provide that, in case the seat of any member of this House is vacated for any cause and the writ for the election of a new member is- not issued within a prescribed time, it shall be the duty of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to issue the writ for a new election.
All that the Prime Minister has to do today is to make that a Government Bill. As the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) said the other day, it ivould go through, certainly without any opposition on .this side of the House, and I do not think there would be any opposition on the other side.
It is a Bill which is very much needed just now. We have six vacancies throughout the country and those vacancies ought to be filled; there is no reason why the people of those divisions should be disfranchised. I don't know whether any change has come over the views of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) since 1908. Probably he has overlooked the fact that he entertained such views at that time, but I have now recalled them to his attention and I trust action will be taken in the matter before the House prorogues.
I do not intend to take up the time of the House much longer. It would be practically impossible to traverse in any way the remarks of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. He had already dwelt upon the subjects that he discussed to-day in what I might call his first Budget speech a few days ago, and we also had his views expressed in the various committee stages when he introduced legislation providing for credits to Roumania and other countries. The House is therefore thoroughly familiar with the hon. gentleman's views, and the matters he touched upon have been fairly well discussed previous to this time.
I do not know whether it is well that I should refer to the Winnipeg riots. A condition of things has arisen in Winnipeg which we on this side predicted a few weeks ago. We charged the Government with inefficiency and ineptitude in the handling of this situation. The Government decided that it was time to do something and they

did something which we now see was the wrong thing; they have precipitated action, and we do not know where this is going to lead us. In any event, the whole of the labour organizations throughout the country are up in arms, and it is for the Government to attend to these matters inasmuch as they themselves are responsible from the very inception for the present condition of affairs.
May I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by quoting the words of a recent Canadian writer whose advice may be accepted with profit by the Government and by every member of the House. This writer says:
The nations that refuse to learn and inwardly digest, whose statesmen, labour leaders and captains of industry and commerce proceed on their way serenely and imperturbably-the nations undisturbed by the gathering clouds of anarchy, whose leaders have souls so small and vision so narrow that they cannot And the way -out of the well worn rut, whose sole conception of reconstruction is " business as usual." Will they be able to stem the onrushing tide of social unrest that has already swept into the maelstrom the mightiest European Eimpire and is rushing westward with gathering fury, to submerge and envelope other nations? Where in its ruthless path will it encounter the strong, arresting wall of enlightened public opinion reared on the Solid foundation of social justice, against which it will impotently spend its force.
These remarks might well be taken to heart by the .Government and particularly by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), who makes a special study of social questions; and if there he any social unrest just now in the country, I think that hon. gentleman will have to accept his full share of the responsibility owing to the fact that he failed to see and to grasp the import of the situation which is now staring us in the face.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Apparently my hon. friend withdraws what he said. I understood him to say that I had disclosed Cabinet secrets. If the hon. gentleman said so, he said what was not true, for I did not do so. I said nothing in my address
which was not based on knowledge acquired outside the Cabinet.

When I say that, I think I should correct what may be a misapprehension on the part of some: I never expect that we will get back to the value of 1914.
I think that ultimately values are going to be greater than they were, and perhaps it is a God-send to the nations that that should be so after the experiences we have gone through; because if we had to pay the accounts of to-day in the services and goods of five years ago our debts would be double what they are. Hence I do not expect that. But, on the other hand, who will now say that the disturbance which has taken place in the values has reached its limit? The fall in the value of money now represents somewhere between 50 and 60 per cent. Is that all that it is going to fall? That is one question that is now disturbing the business community; that is one reason why wages and prices are not on a fixed basis, and why business is uncertain and in need of Government support, as we grant it is.
Now, in extenuation of, or excuse for the course that the Finance Minister has taken this year in not raising greater taxes and in going so heavily upon loans, it may as well be said at once that good national finance depends upon good trade and good industry-if you have not sound trade and sound industry you cannot have sound national finance. National finance is a superstructure built upon the conditions of business generally, and we all know that these conditions to-day are uncertain, and as I have said, pertufbed. But I take it that what the radicals sometimes say is very largely true, that " politics are the soul of economics." By that they mean that our knowledge of how to do business, of how to make money, of how to produce goods for the benefit of the community, is not allowed to operate without disturbance. There is unavoidable political interference-the levying of taxes, the imposition of tariffs, trade restrictions in the way of patent rights and so on, interfere with just and equitable distribution. In this view politics may justly be said to be the soul of economics. Now we are reaping in large measure the penalties of not having raised more by taxation in the past, and especially are'we now reaping the penalties in this, that our Finance Minister does not know, I believe, where to turn at present for more revenue. He is jealous about letting go imposts in the

shape of tariffs because he does not see just how to replace them; and that is the position, I believe, of most members of this House when they come to considei that question. There are practically five large areas of taxation; youy imposts, or tariffs, your excise, your income tax, your estates duties tax, and possibly, as a last resort, a land tax.
In Canada we have undoubtedly fully developed the tariff taxation; the imposts we have not neglected, whatever else we may have overlooked. Before the war we were probably the only country in our stage of industrial development which was relying wholly upon imposts and excise for all its federal taxation. Indeed, to-day, among the great industrial nations of the world-Great Britain, the United States, France, Australia and New Zealand-we stand with the highest tariff taxation and the lowest income taxation. Now, that being so, I take it that we have not been developing along the proper lines. The war caught us unprepared to embark upon any other method of taxation, and one of my criticisms of the Budget to-day is that the Finance Minister is not now developing the other sources of revenue which he is going to require if he is to do the full duty of a Finance' Minister. What is that full duty? I will read a quotation which sets it out in better word? perhaps than I could use myself?
That great ministers were not those who balanced the national accounts by sparing the national forces while renouncing the politically indispensable outlay, but those who stimulated all the live forces of the nation to cheerful activity, and so employed them to national ends that the state revenue sufficed to meet the admitted political demand.
Now, Sir, we are not doing that to-day,- we are not able to do it. The one field of taxation which I see now open to us and immediately available is one which has always been condemned by English feeling and English practice-and that is a vei.v great extension of our excise 9 p.m. taxation. Some one may ask about the devolution of estates duties. Well, England to-day is raising from that source but three per cent of her total revenue, and England is an older and a much wealthier country than we are. Hence, what can we expect to raise from it? Probably the same proportion,-and then cut that in two or more, because the provinces have already entered upon that field, and we would have to make the duties exceedingly high if we were to get anything out of such taxation.
Turn again to the question of land taxes. My own feeling is that of the Finance Min-

istur, that it is not advisable for the federal power to enter upon that field as long as there is any other recourse for us. It is better, more easily, and more economically administered by the municipalities and the provinces, and it is more germane to their finances. It seems to me that we should endeavour to come to some understanding with the provinces and get them, in lieu of our touching that field, to give us the income field of taxation. However, if that cannot be done, we are going to have to consider entering upon the taxation of land values in some fashion, and if we do that it is going to take us about three years at least to put it into any kind of shape so as to get any considerable amount of revenue out of it. I know that in our own province of Manitoba we put upon the statute book a Patriotic Duty Tax. It took us about a year and a half to equalize the assessments so that the weight of that tax would fall fairly upon all parties in the province. If it took a year and a half to equalize the taxation of one province alone, how long would it take us to get returns to equalize the taxation of the nine provinces of the Dominion?
I wish now to make an application of what I have been saying. For my own part, I have with regret to depart from the Government on this occasion. The promise, implied at least, is being held out to us that the tariff will be revised downwards. I get no explicit promise of it, I do not expect an explicit promise. Then I turn to the reductions contained in the Budget and weigh them out, and what am I bound to conclude? In the first place, that the situation is one in which they cannot carry out that downward revision. It is going to be impossible next year to give us that, because this year and in past years they have not developed those areas of taxation which would enable us now to shift the incidence of our tariff taxation. I think that is absolutely clear upon the face of it.
Again, let us look at what has been done in the way of the reduction of duties, especially with regard to agricultural implements. Here the vested interests of the manufacturers of Canada has been the basis of action; the reduction of tariff has been bought from them, and the price is a reduction of freight rates. It is absolutely indefensible, as a matter of finance, to mix up tariffs with freights. The manner in which this duty on agricultural implements has been dealt with shows that the Government is not headed toward a reform of the tariff in accordance with the demands of
nineteen-twentieths of the people who sent me here and in line with my own political record in the past and what my own common sense suggests. Two of the men whom I last saw before I came back from my home last May were the president of the Conservative Association and the gentleman who would have been the Conservative candidate at the last election had we not had Union Government. They both told me that this question must be pressed to a finish; that we must not be slow to demand a reform which, in the West as well as in the East, is fundamental to reconstruction.
Why was there not an absolute elimination of the duty on cement, especially in view of the fact that the capitalization of the cement merger is largely water?-I I won't say what proportion. We are told by everybody that the cement people are well able to go into the markets of the world and take care of themselves; yet the people are still charged a duty of eight cents a barrel on cement. The manner in which the Government has dealt with this cement business is an indication of its intentions. The cement business is absolutely able to stand upon its own feet, but it is not being asked to do so; it, too, must be protected. How must I judge, then, of the future intentions of the Government with regard to the tariff if that is the line which they take now? As to the question of oils, perhaps the Western members asked what was not perfectly in line with principle. I think that the farmer ought to pay taxation upon operating costs just as well as any one else, but it is a severe tax. They asked for a reduction of the duty largely because consumers of oil in Canada are in the hands of the oil trusts of the United States, and they did not see any reason why the imposition of duties should be used as a pretext for the raising of the price to Canadian consumers.
I now come to the question of the duties on wool, cotton and leather goods. You will understand that we asked that the duties be taken off only the commoner varieties of these goods, and that a limited reduction be made a matter involving, perhaps, a $3,000,000 reduction of revenue, which would undoubtedly have been made up twice over by reason of the increased revenue derived from the importation of larger quantities of that class of goods. This would have done something to reduce the cost of living. Here are some significant figures which I got together recently for purposes of comparison. In the United States, out of an importation of $225,000,000 worth of wool.

$ 199,000,000 was free of duty, $26,000,000 [DOT]dutiable, and $9,000,000 was collected by way of duties thereon. In Canada, out *of an importation valued at $30,000,000, $6,000,000 was free, and we collected about $6,500,000 by way of customs duties upon the remainder. Do you wonder, therefore, that in Canada we are paying $18 or $19 per capita in tariff taxation, while last year the people of United States paid only $1.69 per capita? The Finance Minister said this afternoon that we cannot raise our income taxes beyond what they are in United States. But you cannot induce people to come here and live here if you ask them to pay from ten to fifteen times as much "by way of duty upon these goods as they would pay if they lived in the United States, because no natural obstacle prevents their returning to the country whence they came.
Let us look for a moment at the duties upon cotton goods Of course, the United States produce a great deal of their cotton, but their total importation was about $81,000,000, and ours was about $56,000,000, because we have to buy a great deal of our raw material. Of that raw material about $21,000,000 came in free, but we pay a duty * of $9,000,000 on about $35,000,000. The United States, as I say, have their own raw material, but they import some special kinds of material for their own purposes, and of the $81,000,000 worth of cotton and cotton goods which they imported, $38,000,000 were free and $43,000,000 dutiable, the customs revenue from this source amounting to about $14,000,000. It must be remembered that United States duties are not on a flat rate basis, as ours are, they are not, for instance, 25 per cent upon all classes of a given commodity, the duties are scaled from 5 per cent upwards-74 per cent, 10 per cent, 101 per cent, and so on, so that the dearer the goods, the higher the duty, and vice versa. I cannot see why that principle is r.ot a good one to introduce into our own tariff.
With regard to leather goods, the comparison is yet more striking. In the United States, of an importation valued at about $22,000,000, $14,000,000 was free and $8,000,000 dutiable. In Canada none of the importation is free; the $9,000,000 worth is dutiable. If the principle enunciated by the Finance Minister is right, that we cannot raise our income tax above what it is in United States, how can we expect to retain population when we impose duties which are ten, twelve, or fifteen times as high >as the duties upon similar articles in United States? Our Government, are

conscious of the fact that capital is mobile and that it is free to move out, but they forget that labour is just as mobile and just as free to move out. This is one of the things that has been retarding the growth of Canada.
I was caused to look into the question of unemployment last year on account ol certain inquiries which weTe made by the Committee on Agriculture. Some have wondered why the farmers of Ontario, after voting so strongly for Union Government, were so critical of Union Government six months after its formation. I do not know whether all hon. gentlemen know that the farmers of Ontario found themselves last spring 27,500 hands short of their requirements in connection with the spring work upon the farms. Only three or four years ago the Finance Minister said that our whole fiscal system had been revised with a view to building up our industries. That is true; that is the purpose of a high tariff, and it has effected its purpose in Canada. We have much more wild land than United States, being a younger community; our population, urban and rural, is distributed almost exactly as is the population of United States. But our fiscal policies have not been so designed as to cause the people to take advantage of the undeveloped natural resources which lie at our doors and offer to our people a means of profitable employment.
My great quarrel with the tariff is this, that you tax profitable businesses for the support of unprofitable businesses. That argument cannot be denied; it is admitted that that was the purpose at the beginning. It is only in the last stage that this may not be so, then the business is presumed to have become a national asset able to give us goods at world prices without protection. And the last stage in Canada-with protection continued-has now lasted how many years, and how many more years will it last if there be not resistance to the principle of protection?

Therefore, to make my position clear, I want to state first that I think the criticisms that have been coming from honourable members on your

left, Mr. Speaker, as regards the Prime Minister's absence and his work overseas have been absolutely uncalled for.
